summary: The assessee assessee was a Hindu undivided family and the income tax Officer assessed the loss to the tune of Rs.2,00,000/ . The Income Tax Officer held that the net wealth of the assessee was not taxable in view of section 2(f) of the Act. On appeal by the Revenue, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer and dismissed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the revenue that the income of the deceased was taxable in the hands of the family and not as a result of the partition between the assessee and his wife and his sons. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Income tax Officer has not given any reasons for arriving at the conclusion that the assets were not taxable under section 2 (f) or section 2 of the Indian Income Tax Act. [703E] 2. The High Court was right in holding that the assessee had no income to pay the net income of his deceased wife and the amount of the net assets was not liable to be assessed as income tax. [803F] 3. The assessee 's case is that the total wealth of a Hindu Undivided Family is taxable only under section 4(1) (f). The High court has rightly held that it was not a capital asset but an asset which is capable of being used for the purpose of earning profits. [903E F] 4. In view of the fact that the property in question was not taxed under section 3(1)(f), the assessee could not be assessed to income tax under section 5(1).

The respondent was appointed as a Junior Engineer in the Department of Revenue, Punjab. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Engineer on the basis of his seniority in the cadre of Assistant Engineers. The respondent was promoted as Assistant Engineer and he was given a charge sheet under Rule 16(1) of the CCS (CCA) Rules 1965. The disciplinary authority held that the respondent had been guilty of misconduct, and dismissed him from service. The Tribunal held that there was no evidence to show that the charges were proved against him. The High Court also held that since the charges proved against the respondent were proved, the order of dismissal was not justified. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had committed an error in holding that the charge sheet was vitiated by any error apparent on the face of record and that the findings recorded by the disciplinary authority are based on no evidence. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court has not properly appreciated the evidence on record and has come to a conclusion that the order passed by the Disciplinary Authority is vitiated by error apparent in law. [797C] 2.2 In the instant case, the Tribunal was justified in holding the charge of misconduct against the Respondent. [ 797F G] 3.3 The High Courts have not properly considered the evidence and come to the conclusion that there were no material on record to show whether the charges had been proved or not. [897G H] 4.4 In view of the above, the High Court was right in holding t he Tribunal was wrong in holding th at the disciplinary proceeding against the appellant.

The appellants were the tenants of a portion of the property in dispute. The suit was decreed by the trial court on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation as it had been filed within time and that the plaintiff was not entitled to any relief under Order VI Rule 17 C.P.C. for possession of the said portion. The appellants filed an appeal before the High Court which dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiffs were not entitled for possession on the date of the suit, and that they had no right to claim any relief in respect of the portion of it. In appeal by special leave, the appellants contended that the High court was wrong in holding that there was a bar under Order VII Rule 17 CPC to entertain a suit for possession. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of Order VI, Rule 17 are not applicable to a suit filed within the time and the suit must be dismissed on the basis of the provisions contained in Order VII, Rule 11 C. P.C., and that it is only when the plaintiff has obtained possession of that portion of his property or the portion thereof is sought to be evicted from the portion which he was entitled to under Order VIII, Rule 16 C.p.C.. [697B] 2. The High Court was right in holding the suit as barred by time and not on the facts of the case. [698D E] 3. In view of the fact that the defendants were not in possession of any portion of their property, the suit filed by them was not maintainable. [797C D] 4. The plaintiff had no locus standi to file a suit under Order IX, Rule 13 C.Ps. for recovery of possession of some portion of land. The defendants were entitled to claim relief under section 7(1)(c) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. [898D F] 5. In the instant case, the plaintiff had not obtained any right in respect thereof. He was not in actual possession of a part of the land. He could not be said to have been in actual physical possession of it or that he was in actual occupation of it and that he had no title to the property. [998D] 6. The plaintiffs were entitled only to claim possession of portion of that property. They were also entitled to the relief under Section 7(2) of Order VII CPC.

The petitioners are engaged in the manufacture of sugar and other allied products. They were employed as a daily wage worker in the State of Himachal Pradesh. The petitioners were engaged in various industries in the Union of India. Their services were terminated by the Corporation on the ground that they had been engaged in any industry in the area of their jurisdiction. The Corporation filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the validity of the termination order and the High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the petitioners are entitled to be paid wages as per the provisions of the Act, and that they were not entitled to any relief under Article 32 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The State Government has been empowered to fix the pay scale of workers in the Corporation and the petitioners have been working in the same area. [630F] 2. The Court cannot interfere with the decision of the High Courts on the basis of the materials placed before it by the parties. It is not possible for this Court to interfere with such a decision. [730G H; 730A B] 3. The question whether the petitioners were entitled to the relief under Articles 32 and 31 of the constitution is not a matter which has to be decided in each case. [831C D] 4. The High Court has rightly held that the petitioner are entitled for the relief claimed by them. [930F G] 5. In view of the fact that the Corporation has been discharging its functions as a regular wage worker, it is not necessary to interfere in such matters. [1030G] 6. The writ petition is dismissed.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to life imprisonment for the offence of murder punishable under section 201 I. P.C., and sentenced them to life life imprisonment. The High Court acquitted all the accused on the ground that they had been falsely implicated in the case and that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge against them. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was not justified in interfering with the conviction of the accused under section 304 I.PC. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The prosecution has failed to establish the charge under section 306 read with Section 34 I P. C., and the evidence of the witnesses examined by them is sufficient to prove that they were falsely implicated. [797C] 2. The trial court was right in holding that the accused had committed the offence punishable under sections 302 readwith section 34, I.T.P., and that there was no evidence on record to show that the deceased had been murdered by the accused. [ 797F G] 3. In view of the fact that the charge was not proved beyond reasonable doubt, it is not necessary for us to interfere with the judgment of acquittal under section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. [897C D] 4. The conviction of all the appellants under section 307 read with sections 34 I I.A. and 302 read together with section34 I.D., are set aside. [997F H] 5. In the instant case, the High court was justified in holding the charge of murder under section302 I.C.. and sentenced each of them to death. The sentence of imprisonment for life is reduced from one year to two years.

The appellant, a widow of the deceased, filed a suit for possession against the respondent and his mother. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the appellant had failed to prove that she was in possession of the properties as her husband and that the properties were not ancestral property. The High Court held that the evidence of the appellant was not reliable and that it was not proved that she had been in possession and that she could not be said to have been in actual possession of properties. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the document was not a genuine one and that there was no proof of the fact that the respondent had failed in his presence. The document was a genuine document and it was proved that the will was executed by her husband on the basis of which the will had been executed. Held further, that there is no evidence to show that the testator had not been in physical possession of any properties. The appellant could not prove that he had been given the property as his wife and that he was in actual physical possession. The fact that she did not know the will would not be sufficient to establish that she has been in continuous possession of those properties. It is true that the execution of the will is a genuine proof of fact but it is not necessary for the Court to prove the fact of the execution. But the evidence must be such as to enable the Court, to draw an inference from the circumstances of each case. The presumption of the truth can be drawn only if there are two circumstances, namely, (i) that the Will was a true one and (ii) that it is a true document.

The appellant company was a registered dealer under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The sales tax authorities held that the sales were not taxable in view of Entry No. 4 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and that the goods were liable to tax under Entry No., 4 of the First Schedule to that Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the entry was not taxable as it stood before the amendment of the Constitution, and that entry was a "goods" within the meaning of Entry 2(b) of List I of the Second Schedule to this Act. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended: (1) that the entries were not 'goods '; (2) that entry could be treated as "goods ' within the definition of "goods". HELD: (i) The entry was an "goods " and therefore, Entry No.. 4 of Schedule to it was a 'goods" under Entry 2 of List III. [707E] (ii) The entries in the First schedule to the Act were not "goods", but were "goods within the ambit of Entry 3 of List 1 of the Third Schedule to which the entry had been made. [807F G] (iii) The High court was right in holding that entry in the Second schedule to this Constitution did not fall under Entry 3 and that Entry No, 4 of Part I of Schedule II to the Sales Tax Acts were not a "sale" within Entry 2. [907E F] (iv) The words 'goods' in Entry No,. 4 of First Schedule are used in the sense of "any goods". In the present case, the entry in question was an 'goods " within the purview of Entry 1 of List IV.

The petitioners who were engaged in mining operations in the State of Gujarat, were granted a mining lease for the period from 1.4.1989 to 31.3.1990. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said grant on the ground that they had been granted mining leases for the purpose of mining operations and that the said provisions were ultra vires the Constitution. The High Court held that the impugned Act was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution and that it violated Articles 14 and 19 of the constitution. Allowing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The impugned Act is not violative of article 14 of Constitution. [703F] 2.2 The impugned Rules are ultra vires Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the articles of the people. It is a well settled principle that the State cannot impose any tax on mineral rights in respect of minerals which are not covered by Article 14 or Article 19. [803G H; 803A B] 3.3 The impugned rules are ultra violative of Articles 14 or 19 of Constitution and are therefore void. [903B C] 4.4 In the instant case, the petitioners had been given mining leases in respect whereof the petitioners were granted mining lease by the State Government for the purposes of mining operation. They had been paying royalty at the rate of Rs.5 per sq. meter. The impugned notification was issued under section 3(1) of the Gujarat Minor Minerals Concession Rules, 1957 and the said rules are not ultra vires Article 14. [403B D] 4:4 The impugned notifications are ultra ultra vires articles 14 and 21. [603C] 5:5 The impugned Notification is ultra vires article 19 of constitution.

The appellant was a Hindu Religious Trust. The appellant was the trustee of the temple and the appellant was appointed as a trustee under section 3(1) of the Madras Hindu Religious Trusts Act, 1950. The respondent filed a suit for declaration that the appellant had been appointed as an agent of the appellant and that he was entitled to be appointed as the trustee under the Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent was not entitled to any appointment as a manager under section 4(1). In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant 's right to hold office in the temple is an absolute right and must be determined by the Commissioner of Endowments. [601 B] (ii) The right to receive office in a temple is not an absolute one but it is an independent right. It is an exclusive right which is conferred on the trustee to hold the office in that temple. [702 C D] (iii) The expression 'office ' means any office which is held by him for the purpose of carrying on the business of the trust. The word 'office " means any place which is not held by himself for the purposes of carrying out the objects of the Trust. It does not mean that the office is held in a particular manner and it is not so held. [802 C] (iv) The term 'office" has been defined in section 2(1)(a) to mean any place where the office of an agent is held for the benefit of the person who holds the office. It means any other place which can be held by a person who hold the offices. [903 D E] (v) The word "office" means any part of the office which has been held for that purpose.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the accused of all the charges. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed to prove the case against him beyond reasonable doubt and that the evidence of PW 1, who was a witness to the occurrence, was not reliable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court has rightly held that the testimony of PW 2, who is an eyewitness to the incident, was unreliable. [601 B] In the instant case, the prosecution failed to establish the case beyond reasonable doubts and therefore the conviction of the accused under section 34 of the Indian Penal Code cannot be sustained. [702 C] The High Courts have rightly held the testimony against the appellant beyond reasonable suspicion. [803 D] The evidence of PWs 1 and 2 is not reliable, but it is a rule of prudence that the Court should not interfere with the conviction on the basis of the evidence adduced by the prosecution. [903 B] The prosecution has failed to show that the accused had been falsely implicated in the crime. [1002 D] In view of the fact that PW 1 was an eyewitness, it is difficult to accept the testimony given by PW 1. [1102 C E] The conviction under section 201 read with Section 34 I P.C., is not based on any evidence. [403 B C] In order to prove its case beyond doubt, the Court must be satisfied that the circumstances proved against him are such as to justify his conviction.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family and the income of the deceased was assessed to tax under section 10(1) (a) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer held that the income had been assessed to income tax under the Indian Incometax Act, 1961. He also held that in view of the provisions of section 10 (1) of that Act the income was liable to be assessed to be income from the family and that the assessee was not entitled to any deduction under section 11(1). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The income of a Hindu joint family is liable to tax only if it is assessed to business in India. It is not necessary for the Income tax Officer to decide whether the income has been assessed or not. [615 F] (ii) The expression "income from the business" in section 10 of the Act means income from which the income is assessed and not profits. In the present case, the income from a family was assessed only if the income were assessed to his own use. It was not necessary that the Incometax Officer should have taken into account the income received by him from the deceased. The income from such a family could be assessed only on the basis of the income which he had received. [715 F G] (iii) The word "income" in the section is used in the sense in which it occurs. It does not mean that income must have been assessed for the purpose of assessment or reassessment. In other words, the expression " income from any business" has to be construed as a reference to the income and not to the profits of the family. [815 F H] (iv) The words "income received by a Hindu family" in sub section (1)(a) are used in section 12(1)(b) of this Act. It means income received from a Hindu Hindu undivided families. In such cases, the Income-tax Officer has to decide what income is liable for tax under that Act.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State and were appointed to the service of the Government of India. The petitioners were selected by the Public Service Commission for appointment to the posts of Assistant Engineers. They were appointed on the basis of a competitive examination conducted by the Government. The Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Act, which provided that the State Government shall appoint an officer not below the rank of Assistant Engineer in the service or post of Assistant Executive Engineer to fill up the vacancies in the posts specified in the said notification. The notification was published in the Gazette on March 1, 1959. The respondents were appointed by the Central Government under section 4(1). They challenged the validity of the notification and the validity thereof. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the petitioners had not been appointed as Deputy Engineers to the post of Deputy Executive Engineer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the notification was invalid because the petitioners were not appointed as a Deputy Executive Engineers in their respective posts, and that the impugned notification was bad because the notification did not provide for any provision for appointment of Assistant Sub Engineers to fill the vacancies. HELD : (i) The notification issued under section 6(1)(a) of Act was valid because it was invalid on the ground that the said notifications were invalid because it had been issued in exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of the Andhra Nadu State and Subordinate Services (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1956. [601 B] (ii) The petitioners had no right to be appointed as an Assistant Engineer under the Government and that they were not entitled to any appointment on the grounds that they had been appointed in their own capacity. They could not be denied the right to hold the posts which were not included in the notification. [702 C D] (iii) The impugned notification is invalid because, it was issued in pursuance of the provisions of section 3 and the petitioners are entitled to the same rights as they had already been appointed on a regular basis.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the appellant of all the charges. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant had been guilty of an offence under section 201 read with Section 34 I P.C. and sentenced by the trial court. He was not convicted for any offence under sections 201 readwith section 34. [401 B] (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that the appellant was guilty of the offence under s.201 read with s.34. [501 C] (iii) The prosecution had failed to prove that the articles recovered were stolen or that the article was stolen or destroyed. The appellant could not be convicted for an offence punishable under section 120 read with sections 34 and 201 read together. [602 B] In the instant case, the appellant had not been convicted for the offence of theft. He had not proved that he had been arrested on the basis of a statement made by him in his presence. The fact that the police had recorded the statements of the witnesses was not established. [703 D] (iv) The evidence of the prosecution was not sufficient to prove the appellant guilty under section201 readwith s. 34 I I. P. C. and the High Court was right in convicting him for an offences punishable under sections 302 readwith Section 34. The conviction of the appellant under section 307 read with Sections 34 and201 read together was therefore illegal.

The appellants were tried for offences under sections 323, 504 and 506 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court dismissed their application on the ground that the order was not passed in accordance with law and that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to pass an order which could be made only after the order had been passed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court had no power to pass any order which might be made under section 323 of the Code, because the Magistrate did not give a notice to the appellants to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. HELD : (i) The High court has no jurisdiction in the matter of an application for leave to appeal against an order passed by the Magistrate under section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code. [808 C] (ii) The order was passed without giving a notice and opportunity to show why he had been dismissed from services. It is not open to the High court to pass such orders as it may deem fit. [908 D] (iii) The Magistrate has no power under section 319 of the Cr. P.C., to pass a order which may be made in accordancewith law. [1008 C E] (iv) The power of the High Courts is not confined to an order made by the Sessions Judge, but only to the order passed under section 321 of the Act. [1108 D F] (v) In the instant case, the HighCourt had no authority to pass the order in accordance therewith.

The appellant was charged with murder under section 302 I.P.C. for having committed the murder of one Ram Singh, who had been convicted by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 307 I. P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had not been given a chance to explain his evidence in court. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant had not given any opportunity to explain the circumstances of the case, and that the circumstances were not established by the prosecution. HELD : (i) The High Courts should have accepted the evidence of the witnesses on the basis of which they could be relied upon. [601 B] (ii) The evidence of a witness is not sufficient to prove his guilt. It is only when the witness has stated that he was given a reasonable opportunity to meet the defence, and the circumstances are such as to enable him to explain it in court, and if the witness is given a fair chance to meet his defence, the High Court should have rejected the evidence on the sole ground that the witness had not stated that the witnesses were present at the time of the occurrence. [701 B C] (iii) The appellant was not given a opportunity to cross examine the witnesses in court and the High Courts had rightly accepted the testimony of the witness. [802 D] (iv) The statement of the appellant under section 313 Cr. P., is not admissible as evidence. It must be proved that he knew the appellant at the relevant time, and was therefore guilty of murder.

The respondents, who were the contesting candidates, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the election of the appellants to the Municipal Council, Jabalpur. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the election was vitiated by non compliance with Rule 3(1) (a) and (b). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petitions in view of the provisions contained in Rule 3 (1) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The writ petition is dismissed. [632C] 2. In the instant case, the High Courts have not considered the merits of the claim made by the appellants and the High courts have failed to consider the merits on merits. [733D] 3. The petitioners had filed a Writ Petition in the Supreme Court challenging that order. They were not entitled to challenge the validity of the election. They had also filed a petition in this Court for quashing the election on the ground that the same was vitiated because of non compliance of Rule 3 of the Rules. [833C] 4. The respondents have not been able to show any cause or justification for the delay in filing the writ Petition. They have not produced any material before the High Power Committee which had taken into consideration the merits and merits of their claim. They are entitled to raise all contentions in support of their claims. [933C D] 5. The petition is allowed. The order of the High High Court is set aside. The matter is remitted to the HighCourt for fresh decision on merits after giving opportunity to the parties to lead evidence.

The respondent company was a company carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar. The company was prosecuted for offences under section 120B, I.P.C. and section 120 B read with section 34(1)(a) of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court held that the company had committed an offence under section 121B read with s.34(1) (a) and section 109(2) of that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent company that the offence under sections 120B and 109(1), I. P.C., was not a case of criminal breach of trust and therefore, the High Court should have held that there was no breach of the trust and that the prosecution had failed to prove that the accused had committed any offence under s.120 B readwith section 34 (2) (b). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Courts were right in holding that the charge under section 201(1A) was not proved. [630 H] In the instant case the prosecution failed to establish that the respondent had committed a breach of any trust and the company was guilty of criminal misconduct. It is true that the High Courts have held in favour of the accused that the charges were proved. But it is true, that the evidence adduced by the prosecution did not show that the directors of the company were guilty of the offence of criminal misappropriation. The fact that the Directors had committed the offence does not make any difference to the question whether the company has committed a criminal breach. [730 H; 730 A] In view of the provisions of section 120A, I., P. C., it is clear that the Court should not interfere with the order of conviction and sentence passed by the High court.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court held that the offence of murder was not committed in the course of a criminal trial, but was not tried by a competent court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the offences of murder were not committed within the meaning of section 3(1) (c) of the Act and therefore the provisions of section 4(1)(d) of that Act could not be invoked in view of the fact that the trial had been conducted by a court subordinate to it. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the provisions contained in section 4 (1) of this Act were not applicable to the case because the offences committed by the accused persons were not tried as defined in section 3 (1). The provisions of sections 4 and 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act are not applicable in the case of a prosecution under the Act. The provisions contained therein are not intended to be used in the same manner as they are intended to give effect to the provisions which are inconsistent with the provisions made by the Act, but are intended only to give them the benefit of the provisions. It is true that the legislature has not intended that the procedure prescribed by section 4 should be followed in a particular case and it cannot be said that the rules of natural justice have been violated. The object of the legislation is to prevent the abuse of power or to secure the ends of justice, but it does not mean that the Legislature has intended that no person should be prosecuted for an offence under the Prevention Of Corruption Act. It would be a case where the legislature had intended that in order to prevent abuse of powers or to prevent miscarriage of justice the Court must have regard to the object and purpose of the enactment. The legislature is not bound by its own rules but it has only intended that such action should be taken against the accused person. The Legislature cannot be expected to do so under section 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, because it was not possible for the High Courts to act in a manner which would cause serious prejudice to the accused. It must be remembered that the power conferred by section 3 is not intended only in cases where there are special reasons for doing so. The power conferred on the Court under section 5(1), therefore, cannot be exercised in a case of prosecution under section 6 of the .

The appellant was appointed as a Professor in the Department of Medical Education. He was promoted to the post of Professor in Central Hospital, Delhi on January 1, 1964. The appellant was selected for the post in question by the Selection Committee and he was appointed to the said post on January 2, 1964 on the basis of his seniority in the service. The Selection Committee recommended the appellant 's name for promotion to the higher post of Lecturer in the Central Hospital. The recommendation of the Selection committee was accepted by the Government of India. The Government of Delhi issued a notification dated March 3, 1964 inviting applications from eligible candidates for promotion as Professor in a Department of Health and Family Welfare, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare. The said notification was challenged by the appellant on the ground that the appellant had been appointed to a post in the same Department and that he had not been appointed as Professor. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Selection Board had no power to make any selection for promotion of Professor or Professor in any Department, Ministry or of Health. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the selection made by the selection committee was invalid because the appellant was not appointed as an Professor in an Department of medical Education and was entitled to be considered for promotion under the said notification. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The selection committee had no jurisdiction to make a selection for appointment to the posts in question. [630F] 2.1 The Selection Board has no power or authority to make selection for the posts of Professor and Professor in another Department of Government of Punjab. It is not open to the appellant to contend that the appointment made by him was invalid merely because he had been selected for promotion on the recommendation of a Selection Committee. [730F G] 2(a) The Selection Commission has no jurisdiction in making selection for a post which is not a post under the Central Government. It has no authority to do so. [831C D] (b) The appellant ' was appointed by the Central Medical Council on January 3, 1966 and he had also been promoted as Professor on January 4, 1964 and his name was included in the list of selected candidates. He is not entitled to any promotion under that notification. [932F G; 934A B] (c) The selection made in pursuance of the notification dated April 3, 1965 was invalid. [1031C E] 2.(a) In the instant case, the Selection Commission had no authority or power to appoint a Professor on the recommendations of the selection Committee. The appointment of the Professor was invalid as it was not a matter of right. [1132F H] (d) The High court has rightly held that the post which he was selected by the State Government was not an appointment under the Union Government and the appellant could not be considered to be an Professor on that recommendation. [431C G] (e) The appointment made in favour of the respondent was invalid inasmuch as it had no statutory force or power. [532F] (f) The post which the appellant is appointed to another post under Central Government is a post within the meaning of article 12 of the Constitution and the same cannot be said to have been made by an authority other than the State.

The workmen in the present case were employed by the appellant company for a period of five years. The workmen claimed that they were entitled to wages for the period of their employment as a result of which they were paid bonus at the rate of Rs. 10,000 per month. The Tribunal held that the workmen were entitled only to wages on the basis of the formula laid down in the Industrial Disputes Act and not on the ground that they had been paid bonus under the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the formula was applicable to the case of the workmen as a whole, and that the Tribunal erred in holding that the wage structure was not a fixed wage and that there was no justification for the Tribunal to interfere with the award. HELD : (i) The formula was applied only to the cases where the workmen had been employed by them for a long period of time. The formula is applicable to all cases where there has been a change in the wage pattern, and not to the other cases where it is applied to the particular case. [601 B] (ii) The Tribunal erred on the evidence that the wages were paid at the rates fixed by the Government for the purpose of fixing the wage. The tribunal was therefore right in holding the formula as a part of the wage, and the Tribunal was justified in holding it as a full wage. [702 C D] (iii) The principle laid down by this Court in the case referred to in the judgment is not applicable to cases where an industry has been employed for a short period of two years or more, but has been paid at a rate higher than the minimum wages fixed by it.

The respondent assessee, a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax under section 10(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer held that the income of the assessee was not taxable in view of section 5A of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1961 and that the assessment was bad for non compliance with section 5 A of the Act. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice under section 5(1). The High Court held that section 5B of the 1922 Act did not apply to the facts of the case. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The notice under sub section (2) of section 4A was not a notice within the meaning of section 10 and therefore it could not be said that the notice was not served on the assessee. [707 D] (ii) The High court was in error in holding that the Income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to proceed with the assessment under section 7A of 1922 Act. [807 B C] (iii) The order of the High court is set aside and the matter remitted for fresh decision on merits. [907 D E] (iv) In the present case, the notice did not contain any particulars regarding the income or the income from which the assessee had been assessed. The notice was served on him within the time prescribed by section 5 of the 1961 Act. It is true that the assessee has not given a copy of the order to the Incometax Officer as required under section 4 A of 1922.

The appellant company was a registered firm carrying on business in the Indian trade of which the appellant was a partner. The appellant, who was a member of the Indian Trade Union, applied for a certificate under section 10(1) (a) of the Income tax Act, 1922, to the Income Tax Officer, Madras, for a declaration that the appellant had no right to continue in the business of the company and that the said firm was not liable to be assessed to income tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the firm was a Hindu undivided family and that it was not an individual, and that therefore the appellant could not be assessed under section 5(1)(a) (iii) of that Act. On appeal by certificate, Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the assessee was a 'person ' within the meaning of section 2(b) of Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1948, and as such the appellant did not fall within the definition of "person" under section 2 (c). The question whether the appellant is an individual or not must be decided by the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner in the present case. Held, further, that in view of the provisions of section 5 (1) of this Act, the appellant 's right to claim a certificate was not available to him under section 11(1). The appellant could only be assessed as an individual and not by the Incometax Officer. The question for determination was whether the firm had been registered or not. Held further, further that the provisions in section 5 were applicable to the case of a Hindu joint family.

The appellant, a Hindu widow, was the adopted son of one Shri Ramrao. The plaintiff 's suit for partition and separate possession of the properties in dispute was decreed by the trial court on the ground that the properties were not joint family property. The High Court held that the plaintiff had no right to claim partition and that the defendant had no interest in the properties. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the suit was barred under section 4(1)(a) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'family ' is defined in section 2(i) of that Act. It means a family property which has been acquired by the Hindu widow for the purpose of maintenance and maintenance of the family. [601 B] 2. In the instant case, the plaintiff was not entitled to claim any partition or separate possession. The suit was therefore barred under the provisions of section 4 (1)(b) of Act. [702 C D] 3. The question whether the plaintiff ' had no locus standi to file the suit for the partition and the High court was right in holding the suit as barred by section 4 of the Act. In view of the language used in section 4, it is clear that the word ' family ' has been defined in the Act and not in the context of the words 'family'. [703 D] 4. The expression 'family' in section 3(1) (a) means a person who has acquired a right to maintenance or maintenance under the Hindu Law. It is only when the property is acquired by a Hindu wife for the purposes of maintenance, that the property has been purchased by her husband for the benefit of his family. The words ' family' in the section are not used in the sense of the word "family" and the expression 'person who has taken possession of it does not mean a person whose right to maintain the property was acquired by her father. [803 D E] 5. In order to determine whether the property had been acquired for the maintenance or custody of the plaintiff, the High Courts have to examine whether the defendant has acquired any interest in his family and whether the interest of the defendant is a person which has acquired such right. The object of the section is to provide for the transfer of the property by the wife to the husband. [903 D F] 6. In determining whether the word `family ' in section 5(1), it must be shown that the intention of the legislature was to give effect to the intention and not to give a meaning to the words "person who had acquired such interest" in section 6(1). The object is to give an interpretation to the expression "person whose right has been conferred by the Act, and to give the interpretation to it. [1003 G H] 7. In considering whether the expression `family" in the Explanation must be given a meaning which would include a person not who had purchased such property for the time being. The intention of Parliament is that the words `family' should be interpreted in the light of the context in which the word has been used. [1103 G] 8. In construing the expression in section 7(1A) (b), it is necessary to have a meaning given to it in the proviso to section 4 and the intention must be gathered from the context. The proviso to that effect is not intended to give any meaning which may be given to the word used in that proviso. [1203 G G] 9. In interpreting the words of the Explanation, it would be necessary to give meaning to a word in the statute.

The respondent Corporation, a public limited company, was the General Manager of the Life Insurance Corporation. The employees of the Corporation were governed by the provisions of the Employees ' Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952. The Corporation issued a notice to the employees of its employees on the ground that they had been employed in the business of insurance. The notice was served on the employees on January 1, 1956. The respondent Corporation filed an industrial dispute before the Industrial Tribunal alleging that the employees were not entitled to any pension under the Employees' Provident Fund Act, 1948. The High Court held that the employee was not entitled for pension under section 10(2) of the Act and that the Corporation had no power to make regulations in respect of the employees who were employed in a business of banking or other public sector undertaking. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the terms of the notice were not applicable to the employee, and that since the employees had been appointed in a particular manner, they could not be treated as employees of a company under section 12(2). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The terms of section 12 (2) are not applicable in respect to employees who are employed in any business of general public sector undertakings. [703E] 2. The words "any person" in section 12 are not used in the context of the words "other persons" and that they have been employed for a particular purpose. It is well settled that the word "other person" has to be interpreted in its ordinary sense and it should be construed strictly so as to give effect to the intention of the legislature. [803E F] 3. The object of the statute is to provide for the establishment of an industrial concern, and to provide a scheme for the management of the business. It must be understood in the light of the surrounding circumstances that the Act has been enacted to enable the Corporation to make Regulations in respect thereof. The purpose of the legislation is to give a reasonable opportunity to the workmen concerned to meet their demands. [903E G] 4. The scheme of the Provident Fund (Amendment) Act, 1956 which was passed by the Central Government under section 3(2)(a) of that Act has not been extended to the establishment in respect whereof the employees have been appointed. It cannot be said that the object of giving effect to section 12 is to enable them to meet the demands of the workmen. [1003E H] 5. The provisions of section 11 (2)(b) of this Act are intended to provide that the employer shall make regulations for the employees in respect o f the employees employed in an industry, and the employees so appointed shall be deemed to have been in service on the date of their appointment. [1103E C] 6. The word "any other person" is used in section 11(2), which provides that the provisions relating to the conditions of service of a employee shall not apply to any employee who has been employed by him in a banking or financial sector undertaking, and if the employees are not in service for more than one year, they shall be entitled to pension under this Act.

The appellants were members of the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The respondent was a member of the Legislative Assembly and was a Judge of the High Court. He was appointed as a Judge in the Punjab High Court on the recommendation of the Chief Justice of India. The Chief Justice, however, recommended that the Chief Justices should be removed from the office of the Supreme Court. The appellants filed an application before the Chief Minister for contempt of the Court and the ChiefJustice made a statement to the effect that the respondent was not a member in the Legislative Council. The High Court rejected the request on the ground that the order of the Judge was not complied with by the Chief Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High court had no jurisdiction to issue any directions to the Chief Judges and that the contempt of Court should be quashed. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of dismissal is set aside and the matter is remitted back to the High Courts for fresh consideration. [630H; 730A] 2. In the instant case the Chief Ministers had not been removed from his office by the High Judge. He had no power to issue directions to him. He has also not been able to show that he was a Member of the House of the People. The fact that the appellants were not members of any Legislative Assembly is not sufficient to hold that they were members in the House. [730B] 3. In view of the fact that there was no order of removal from the Court, the Chief Chief Justice had no authority to issue a direction to the Judge to issue the directions to be removed. The Judge has no power under article 136 of the Constitution to issue such directions. [831C D] 4. The learned Judges have not been satisfied with the reasons given by the Judge in his order dated November 11, 1975 that the Judge had no powers to issue direction to him to issue summons to the appellants. They are therefore entitled to issue notice to the respondent for contempt. [930G H; 931A] 5. The Court has no jurisdiction under article 226 of the constitution to issue an directions to a Judge to give effect to the order dated December 11, 1976. [1032C D].

The petitioner company was a stock company in the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The petitioner company had been assessed to income tax under section 3(1)(a) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1947 and the Income tax Officer issued notices to the petitioners under sections 8(2), 10(3) and 11(4) of that Act for the assessment year 1948 51. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notices on the ground that they had been issued without jurisdiction as required by section 7(1) of this Act. The High Court held that the notices were not valid and the notices could not be quashed. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that the notice under sections 11(3), 10, 11(5) and 12(4)(a), were invalid as they had not been issued with jurisdiction in respect of the assessment years 1948 51 and 1948 51, and that the proceedings were bad as they were not properly conducted. Held: (i) The notices issued by the petitioners to the petitioner under sections 7(2) and 10(1), were valid and could not have been quashed because they had failed to comply with the provisions of section 7 of the Act. (ii) The notice under section 11(6)(a)(b) was invalid as it did not comply with any provision of section 8(3). (iii) The proceedings in respect Of the assessment Years 1948 51 to 1948 51 were invalid because they were issued without authority of law and that they were invalid. (iv) The petitioners had failed before the Income Tax Officer to show cause why the notices should not be cancelled under section 7, and (v) that the petitioners had not complied with the requirements of section 6(1). (v ) The notices under sections 10(2)(aa), 11(1A) and 13(4), were not invalid because the notices issued under sections 9(3A) were not served on them. (vi) The petitions in respect to the assessment Year 1948 51 could not therefore be dismissed as being barred by section 8 of the Incometax Act, 1961. (vii) The orders passed by the Income Commission under sections 6(2A), 10 and 12 of the Incometax Act were invalid and they were liable to be quashed because the petitioners did not file any return in respect thereof.

The appellant company was registered under the Companies Act, 1956. The respondent company was a registered company in Delhi and its employees were registered under section 3(1)(a) of the . The appellant company filed a complaint before the Income tax Officer alleging that the company had been carrying on business in the manufacture of goods and that the said company was not a "person" within the meaning of section 2(2) of that Act. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was not an 'person" under the provisions of the Companies (Regulation of Supply and Distribution) Act, 1951. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the expression "person", in relation to a business carried on by a company is not defined in the Act as meaning "person". HELD: The word "person ' means any person who carries on business or has been carrying out business in any other manner. It is well settled that the word "persons" must be construed in its ordinary sense and it should be interpreted in its popular sense. [601 B] In the instant case, the appellant company had not been registered under any of the provisions contained in the Companies act. The appellant was a 'person ' within the definition of "person " within the ambit of section 3 (1) (a). It is not disputed that the respondent company had carried on business as a "persons". The word 'person " means any individual or group of persons, but it does not include any person in the definition. [701 B C] In view of the fact that the activity carried on was carried on in the course of trade, the activity of the appellant is not an activity carried by the company.

The appellant was a Hindu undivided family. The income of the respondent was assessed to tax under section 5(1) (a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The respondent claimed that he had been paid a sum of Rs. 1,000/ as compensation for his loss and injury suffered by him in the year 1949 50. The Income tax Officer held that the income of a Hindu joint family was not liable to be assessed under section 4(1)(a) on the ground that it was not a capital expenditure but a capital receipt. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer and dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The income from the family is not liable for any loss or injury suffered in the previous year. It is not a revenue expenditure but an expenditure which is incurred by the assessee for the purposes of his business. [601 F] (ii) The Income Tax Officer was not entitled to claim that the amount of compensation paid by him was a capital income. He could not be said to have been paid in the earlier year as it was a revenue receipt. The question whether the income from a family is liable for tax under the Indian Incometax Act, 1961 does not arise. [701 F G] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the Income Tax officer was entitled to deduct the amount from the income and the expenditure incurred by him for the purpose of his income tax.

The appellants were appointed as Assistant Labour Officers in the respondent State. They were promoted to the post of Assistant Labour Officer on ad hoc basis and they were promoted as Assistant Inspectors on adhoc basis. The appellants were promoted on ad temporary basis on ad interim basis. They had been promoted to a higher post on ad officiating basis. Their promotion was not given effect to by the order dated 5th July, 1983. The respondents filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the said order of the High court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellants were entitled to be considered for promotion as Assistant Inspector on ad permanent basis and that they had been appointed on ad ad hoc service. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the impugned orders dated 5.7.1983 and 5.8.1983 are not applicable to the appellants in the present case. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants have been promoted as Senior Assistant Inspectors in the State of Madhya Pradesh on ad adhoc basis and their promotion is governed by the rules framed under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution of India. [601B] 2.2 The appellants are entitled to get the benefit of the said circular dated 5 th July, 1982. They have been granted the benefit as per the said Circular. [702C D] 3.3 The appellants had been given the benefit in the case of Assistant Inspectors who were promoted earlier on ad regular basis and were promoted later on. The said benefit was not extended to them by the impugned order dated 4th July. 1983. [803D] 4.4 The appellants cannot be denied the benefit under the circular dated 4 th July. 1984. They are entitled for the benefit from the date of their promotion as Senior Assistants in the Central Government. [903F G] 5.5 The appellants, who were appointed on regular basis on the ad hoc appointment, had been granted ad hoc promotion to the said post. They cannot be given the same benefit as they were appointed earlier on regular regular basis.

The Karnataka Motor Vehicles (Regulation of Transport) Act, 1984 was enacted by the State Legislature to provide for the grant of permits to persons who are not registered as a "State" within the meaning of section 2(1)(a) of the Karnataka Motor Vehicle (Regulation and Transport) Amendment Act, 1985. The appellants were granted permits on the basis of their inter State permits in respect of the route in question. They challenged the validity of the permits on various grounds. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the permits had been granted to persons whose inter State permit was not a "state" within section 2 (1)(b) of that Act and that the State Government had no power to grant permits to them, and that it could not be said that the permit was in fact a "public service". The High court held that the Regional Transport Authority had no authority to grant the permits to the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the provisions of section 3(1) (a) were not applicable to the State of Karnataka and that, therefore, the permits granted by the Regional transport Authority could not have been granted in respect thereof. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The State Government has no power under section 3 (1) of this Act to grant a permit to persons other than those registered as "State". [707E] 2. The Regional Transport Authorities are entitled to grant only permits on inter State routes in question and not to any other person who is not registered under the Act. [708F G] 3. The power conferred by section 3 of the Act is a discretionary power which is conferred by the statute. It is a statutory power, which is not intended to be exercised by the Central Government or the State Governments. The object of the section is to provide a special provision for the granting of permits in favour of persons other specified in the permit. [808F] 4. The scheme of the Regional Act is that the grant or renewal of permits should be granted only on inter state routes in respect whereof the permits are granted. It does not mean that the Central Transport Authority has no authority either to grant or renew a permit. The grant or refusal of a permit must be made by the appropriate authority, and not by the concerned Regional Transport authorities. [908F H] 5. The purpose of section 4(1), therefore, is to enable the State Transport Authorities to grant such permits in accordance with the provisions contained in section 3. It has been held that it is a special power which can be exercised only on the inter state route in respect to which the permits have been issued. [1008F F] 6. The question whether the Regional Authority has power to refuse the permit is a matter of discretion and not whether the State or the Central Governments are entitled under section 4. [1108G H] 7. In the instant case, the Regional Regional Transport Officer had no jurisdiction to grant any permits in relation to the route which were granted by it. The permits granted were not in accordancewith the provisions made in section 2 of the .

The respondent was a dealer in the State of Madras. The respondent sold certain goods to the appellant on the ground that the sale was not for a period of one year and that the sales were for a short time. The Sales Tax Officer, after considering the evidence, held that the transaction was for a long time and that it was not a sale within the meaning of section 2(f) of the Act. On appeal by special leave, the High Court set aside the order of the Sales Tax officer and directed the respondent to pay the tax due on the sales effected in the course of inter State trade or commerce. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The provisions of section 3(f)(ii) of that Act are not applicable to a transaction which is for a time, but is for the time being in force. [601 F] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the transactions were for the purpose of the State and that they were for an indefinite period. [702 G H; 703 A B] (iii) The respondent was not entitled to any refund under section 3 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1948. [803 F] In the instant case, the sales in question were for purposes of the Union of India and the State had no power to make a deduction under section 4 of the said Act. [903 A C] (iv) The transactions were not for the purposes of a State but for the reason that they did not fall within the definition of "sale" in section 2 of the Tamil Nadu General Sales tax Act, 1949.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Army and was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been convicted for an offence under section 161(1) of the Bombay Police Act, 1947. The trial court held that the appellant was guilty of misconduct and that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to any relief under article 136 of the Constitution. HELD : (i) The High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain a suit for damages against the appellant, because he was not a member and was not liable to pay any amount due to him. [808 B] (ii) The appellant was not guilty of any misconduct or negligence on his part in discharge of his duties as a member. He was not an employee of the Government of India. He had no right to claim any relief against the Government. [908 C D] (iii) The suit was not barred by time and was therefore barred by the limitation. [1008 B C] (iv) The plaintiff was entitled to the relief under section 165(1)(a) of that Act. [1108 E] (v) The trial Court had rightly held that he was guilty for misconduct and negligence on the part of the appellant. [0908 D] In the present case, the trial court had not properly considered the evidence adduced by the plaintiff in support of his claim. [0808 C] In view of the fact that the trial Court was wrong in holding the suit as barred by section 165 (1)(b) of this Act. The High Courts were right in holding against the State Government. The appellant could not be said to have been guilty of an offence which had been committed by him under section 163(1).

The appellant, a lessee of the land in question, was granted a lease of the lands in question for a period of five years. The lease was granted to the respondents on the ground that the lease was not executed by the lessee and the lease had been executed by him after the expiry of the lease. The respondents filed a suit against the appellant for possession of the said land. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 5(1) (a) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The High Court held that the appellants were not entitled to any relief under section 5 (1)(a). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the suit was barred by limitation as the lease in question had been granted after the period of three years and the appellant had failed to prove that the land was a private forest. Held, that the plaintiff was entitled only to the relief under sections 5(2) (b) and 5(3). The High court was right in holding that it was not proved that the respondents were in possession of any land in dispute. The suit was therefore barred by time as the period for which the lease could be executed was not expired. Held: (i) The appellant had not proved the title of the defendants to the land and the suit must fail on the basis of the evidence adduced by him. (ii) The High Courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the defendants were in actual possession of a land in excess of the prescribed period. (iii) The finding of the High Court was not correct. (iv) The findings of the trial court were based on no evidence and could not be sustained. (v) The respondents had failed in proving the title by adverse possession. (vi) The suit must succeed. (vii) The plaintiff was not entitled for any relief as claimed by him under section 4(1)(b). (viii) The defendants were not in actual physical possession of land in suit and they were in continuous possession of it. (ix) The appellants had failed, before the High court to prove the title on the date of the suit. (x) The trial Court was right when the suit came up for hearing. (xi) The first appellate court was wrong in holding the respondents ' claim that the title was not a private land and that the possession of such land was not delivered within the prescribed time.

The appellant was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been dismissed from services under r. 7(1)(b) of the Kerala Industrial Disputes (Labour and Conciliation) Rules, 1958. The appellant challenged the order of dismissal on the grounds: (i) that the termination of his services was illegal; (ii) that there was no evidence to show that the appellant had been guilty of misconduct or negligence in the discharge of his duties as a result of which he was dismissed; and (iii) that it was not open to the employer to terminate the services of the appellant on the basis of the enquiry report. Held, that the order terminating the services was bad because the termination was illegal and void. The order terminating service was invalid because the appellant was guilty of an misconduct or misconduct in discharge of its duties as such. The termination was not justified because it was made without giving him a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. Held further, that there is no evidence on record to show whether the termination had been made by the employer. The dismissal was illegal because the order was passed without giving any reasonable opportunity of being heard to the appellant and the order dismissing the appellant from service was bad. The fact that the enquiry officer had given a reasonable explanation for the proposed punishment did not make any difference in the nature of the misconduct or misbehaviour. Held also, further, (i). that the dismissal was invalid as it was illegal. The employer was entitled to terminate his services on the finding that the employee had been discharged from service under r 7(2)(b), and that the employer had failed to prove that the workman had been removed from service.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain premises in Bombay, filed a suit for possession of the said premises on the ground that they had been granted a lease of the same premises. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to establish their case and dismissed the suit. In appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the defendants were not entitled to the relief claimed in the plaint. On appeal by certificate, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence on record to show that the plaintiff had failed in his possession or any part thereof. [601 B] (ii) The suit was barred by limitation and the suit was not barred by time. [702 C] (iii) The trial judge was right when he held that there were no evidence to show the existence of a lease. [802 D] (iv) In the instant case, the defendants had failed before the trial court that they were in possession of any premises and that the suit had been filed within time. The High court was right on the view that the trial judge had not committed any error in holding the suit to be barred by law. [902 D E] (v) In a suit instituted under section 14 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, the Court has jurisdiction to try the suit for specific performance of contract. The jurisdiction of the trial Judge is limited only to the question whether the defendants have failed in their possession or not. [1002 D F] (vi) In view of the fact that the High court had committed an error in dismissing the suit, the trial Court was justified in holding it to be a fit case for exercise of its jurisdiction under section 115 C.P.C. and the High Courts were right in rejecting the plaint on the grounds that the defendant had failed. [1102 D G] (vii) The question whether a lease is barred by the provisions of section 115 CPC is not a question of law. It is well settled that the jurisdiction of a civil court is limited to the matter which is within the scope of the jurisdiction conferred on it by the Code of Civil Procedure and the jurisdiction is limited in respect of the matters which are within the jurisdiction. [1202 D H] (viii) The jurisdiction under the Code is limited, when the suit is filed within the time prescribed by section 115 of the Code. It does not mean that the civil court has jurisdiction in respect to the matters specified in the agreement or the agreement.

The respondent was appointed as a Constable in the State of Uttar Pradesh on January 1, 1982. He was appointed to the post of Assistant Commandant in the Government Medical College, Lucknow on the basis of his appointment as a constable in the Central Government. The respondent was confirmed in the post on January 2, 1983. On the expiry of the period of probation he was appointed on January 3, 1984. He continued in service till March 1, 1984 and was paid salary for the period from April 1, 1983 to February 1, 1985. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of termination. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent had been appointed as an constable in Central Government on January 4, 1984 but he continued in the service till May 1, 1986 and was not entitled to any salary for that period. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order terminating his services was illegal and void because the respondent was not a probationer and had been given a right to continue in service after March 1. 1984. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High court was wrong in holding that since the respondent did not join the post he was entitled to salary for this period. [797G] In the instant case, the respondent could not be treated as an probationer and his services were terminated on January 5, 1985 and he continued to hold the post till May 2, 1986. The order of appointment was passed in accordance with law. The termination order was made by the respondent on January 6, 1984 after a period of three years from the date of his joining.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted the accused of the offence under section 304 I. P.C. on the ground that he had been falsely implicated in the case, and that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that the evidence of the witnesses were not reliable and that they could not be relied upon as they were interested witnesses. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court was right in holding the acquittal of the accused on the basis of the evidence adduced by the prosecution. [601 B] In the instant case, the High court had rightly held that the appellant had been guilty of the offences under section 307 I. p.C and sentenced him to death for life. [702 C] The High Courts were right in not interfering with the order of acquittal on the grounds that the trial Court was justified in holding it to be perverse. [803 B] The prosecution case was that the deceased had been murdered by the appellant and his wife, and the appellant was a minor girl. The evidence of P.W. 1, who was the father of the deceased, was not reliable. The prosecution had not proved its case against the accused. The trial Court had rightly convicted the appellant on the sole ground that the witnesses had been interested witnesses in the prosecution case.

The appellant was prosecuted under section 7(1)(a) read with section 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court convicted him under section 5(2) readwith section 7 and sentenced him to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of one year. The High Court dismissed his appeal holding that the appellant had committed an offence punishable under section 3(1) (a) of the Act and that he was not guilty of any offence punishable with imprisonment for life. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that section 7 was applicable to the case of a public servant and that the provisions of section 7 were not attracted to the cases of a person who is in service of the Union or State Government and that since the appellant was not in service, he was entitled to be prosecuted under Section 7(2)(a). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have committed an error in taking cognizance of the offence punishable by section 7 read with Section 7 of Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 1988. [797C] 2.2 In view of the provisions contained in section 7, the High Courts are not competent to take cognizance of a offence under section 8(1). The High court is not competent in taking action under section 6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [897E F] 3.3 The High courts have committed any error in accepting the contention that the charge sheet was not properly served on the appellant and that there was no evidence to show that he had committed any offence under Section 8(2). [798C D] 4.4 In view thereof, the charge sheets are quashed. [997E G] 5.5 The High Judges of the High court are directed to take action under Section 6 of Prevention and Money Llaundering Act, 1894 in accordance with law. [1097F] 2(a) The appellant is acquitted of the charges under section 4(1), read with sections 7(3)(a), 8(4) and 9 of the Criminal Procedure Code. [ 1097E] (b) In view the charge framed against him is proved, he is entitled to take appropriate action under the Act. [100F] (c) The High Judge is directed to proceed with the case in accordancewith law.

The appellant was a member of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. He was elected as a member in the Scheduled Caste. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that he had been disqualified under article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to be declared elected. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the expression "Scheduled Castes" used in article 14 means "Scheduled Tribes". It was further contended that in view of the definition of "Scheduled Caste", the word "Scheduled Tribe" must be construed as a "Scheduled caste". HELD: (i) The word " Scheduled Castes" is not defined in the Act. In the present case, the appellant had been declared elected by the State Government under article 342(1)(b) of the constitution. [808 B] (ii) The expression " Scheduled Caste" used to mean "Scheduled castes". It has been used in the definition that it means "any caste". The word 'Scheduled Castes ' is not used in any sense. In view of this definition, the word ' Scheduled Tribes ' must be understood as a 'Scheduled Tribe ' and it must be given its ordinary meaning. [908 B C] (iii) The words "Scheduled tribes" in article 342 are wide enough to include "any castes". The expression 'Scheduled Caste ' is used in a sense which includes "any tribe". It is not possible to say that the word has been defined in any of the clauses of article 342. [1008 B D] (iv) The definition of ' Scheduled Castes ' means "a person who is a member or a member, whether as a result of caste or community, he is entitled to hold such a post under the Act". In the instant case, it was not possible for the appellant to hold that the words "any tribes" used by the appellant in article 341 were wide enough. [1108 B E] (v) The High court had rightly held that there was no evidence of caste and community as a consequence of caste.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat in Bombay. The complainant, who was the owner of the flat, applied for permission to sell the flat and the Magistrate granted him permission to purchase it. The appellant 's application was rejected by the Magistrate on the ground that the appellant had failed to comply with the provisions of section 3(1) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The High Court held that the complainant had failed in complying with the requirements of section 4(1)(a) and that the offence under section 3 (1) was not attracted. Held, that the provisions contained in section 3 were not applicable to a case where the complainant was a tenant of the building in Bombay and the appellant was not entitled to any protection under section 5(1). The words "any person" in section 2(1), are wide enough to include a person who is in possession of the property. The word "any other person" has been used in the context of the definition of "any such person". In the present case, the appellant ' was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2 (1)(b) and therefore he could not be convicted under section 4 (1). Held, further, that it is well settled that the word "person" in the section must include a tenant who has been in possession. The words used in section 5 (1), therefore, are wide and cannot be construed as including a person whose tenancy was terminated by the landlord.

The appellant company was a registered trade union and its employees were employed in the business of manufacturing and selling goods. The appellant company, a registered association of employees, was engaged in the manufacture of certain articles of electricity, which were used for the purpose of carrying on the business. The workmen were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 10 per month. The Tribunal held that the workmen were entitled to the benefit of the award. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the Tribunal had erred in law in holding that the employees were not entitled to any benefit of this award. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has erred in holding the workmen entitled to a higher wages than what they were entitled under the award and the Tribunal was justified in holding them entitled to get the benefit under the Award. [601C] 2.2 The Tribunal had not given any reasons for rejecting the claim of the workmen that the appellant was entitled to be treated as a registered company. It is well settled that the award is based on an erroneous interpretation of the law and it cannot be said that the tribunal has erred by applying the principle of "equal pay for equal work" in the case of employees who were employed for the purposes of carrying out the business, or that the same was not a mere error apparent on the face of record. [701C D] 2.(a) The Tribunal is justified in taking into account the fact that the industrial dispute was pending before it and the Industrial Tribunal had taken into consideration the fact whether the workmen had been employed for carrying on their business or not, and whether the appellant had been paid wages for the period of their service. [801C E] 3.(b) The award is a reasoned one and does not suffer from any infirmity. It cannot be held that it was based on erroneous interpretation. [902D] (c) The tribunal has failed to take into account all relevant factors including the fact of the matter, which had been taken into account by the appellant in arriving at its decision. [1001C F] 3(a) In the instant case, the Tribunal has not given reasons for refusing to grant the benefit to the workmen. It was not open to the appellant to contend that the Industrial tribunal erred in applying the principles of " equal pay for the past period" and that it had wrongly applied the principle laid down by this Court in the cases of employees of the company. [1101C G] (b) In view of the fact, the Industrial Tribunals have failed to consider the relevant factors which were taken into being consideration while determining the question of the entitlement of the employees to the higher wages. The Industrial Tribunal has also not given a finding that the appellants had been working for more than two years and that they were not in any way entitled to equal pay.

The appellant, a contractor of the respondent, was employed as a contractor in the Mills. The dispute arose between the parties and the appellant was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The appellant filed an application under section 33(2) of the , for the determination of the amount of wages payable to him on the ground that the appellant had not been paid wages for the period during which he worked as a workman. The Labour Court held that the dispute between the appellant and the respondent was not covered by the definition of "workman" in section 2(s) of that Act. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the reference was barred by article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The award of the Labour Court is a decree for the payment of wages for a period of three years and it is not open to the appellant to raise an industrial dispute before the Industrial tribunal.
