[630 F] (ii) The High court was right in holding that there was no evidence on record to show that the respondent had worked as an employee in the Mill during which the appellant worked. The award does not contain any provision for payment of salary for the said period. It is only a decree or order for payment, but it is a final decree and not a decree. [730 F G] (iii) The appellant was entitled to claim wages for that period. [830 H] (iv) The Labour court had no jurisdiction to decide the dispute on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties.

The appellant was convicted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that he had been guilty of an offence under section 420, I.P.C., but the High Court held that the sanction of the Government was not necessary in the case of a public servant. Held, that the prosecution must prove that the appellant had been charged with an offence of criminal misconduct and that the charge was proved by evidence. The sanction of Government was necessary in order to establish that the charges were proved by the prosecution. The prosecution must establish that there was no evidence on record to show that the accused had been convicted under sections 409, I.,P. C. and section 409. Held further, that it was not open to the High court to interfere with the sanction. The appellant was entitled to the benefit of section 409, Indian Penal code. The question whether he was guilty of any offence under sections 420,I.P., Code and section 471 was decided by the High Courts in appeal. Held also, further, the appellant was not entitled to any benefit of the section. The order of sanction was not a judicial order but a judicial decision. The fact that the Government had been given an opportunity to show cause against the sanction must be proved by oral evidence and it could not be said that the order was made in accordance with law. Held: (i) The sanction was necessary for the prosecution of a person who was charged with the offence under the Indian Code and was therefore, required to prove that he was convicted. The charge was not proved by direct evidence. It was not established by evidence that the public servant had been prosecuted under section 471, I..P.c., and that it could be said to have been committed in accordance therewith. (ii) The prosecution was not justified in relying on the evidence of the prosecution witnesses.

The appellant company was a registered firm carrying on business in the State of Travancore Cochin. The Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was extended to the State by section 3(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1961. The assessee claimed that the income of the company had been assessed under section 10(2)(a) of that Act and the income was liable to be assessed under the head "Profits and gains" in the assessment year 1949 50. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the loss suffered by the appellant company could not be said to have been incurred in the business of the appellant. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the losses suffered by it were not income within the meaning of section 10 (2)(b) of Act and that the profits were liable to tax under the Indian Incometax Act. The High Court held that there was no provision for the assessment of the loss in respect of the business carried on by the assessee in the course of its business in Travancore Cochin, but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the expenditure incurred by it was not income and therefore the loss could not have been assessed to tax. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The word "Profits" in section 10 of the Act means "profits and gains". It is well settled that the word "profits" in sub section (1) must be construed as a whole and it should be interpreted in its ordinary sense so as to give effect to the intention of the legislature. [615 F] (ii) The words "Profits or gains" are not used in the context of the words "profits or gains". In the present case, the word 'profits or loss" in clause (a) is used in section 2(1)(b). It is clear that the expression "profits", in sub s.(1) means "Profits, gains and gains", and therefore, the income must be assessed to income tax under section 3 (2) (a).

The respondent company was a registered company carrying on business in the manufacture of its products. The company had been employed as a Company under the provisions of the , and the company had to be treated as a 'industry ' within the meaning of section 2(m) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The respondent company contended that the company was not entitled to any relief on account of the fact that it was engaged in the business of manufacturing its products and that the workmen were not entitled for any relief under the Industrial Dispute Act, 1946. Held, that the Tribunal had erred in holding that the Company was not a ' industry ' within section 2 (m) Of the , as it was not an industry within the definition of 'industry in the Industrial dispute. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal. The order of the Tribunal is set aside and the matter remitted to the Tribunal for fresh decision. The parties are directed to appear before the Tribunal on the date fixed for hearing. The tribunal shall give a reasonable opportunity to the parties to lead evidence in support of their respective contentions. The award of the tribunal shall be set aside. The appellant company was entitled to all the benefits which were admissible to him under the Act. The workmen had been given an opportunity to lead additional evidence in respect of their claim for pension. The employer had not given any reasons for his decision. It is not open to the employer to adduce evidence in rebuttal of its findings on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The company was formed by the company in 1964 and its members were Directors of the company. The Company was a body corporate and it was registered as a company under the . The company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Central Government dated March 31, 1965. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the company had no power to make any inquiry or investigation into the affairs of the Company. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Board had no authority to make an inquiry or investigate into the allegations made against the company and that the order was not in accordance with law. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that section 5(1) of the Act was ultra vires the powers of the Board under article 226 of the Constitution. The power conferred on the Central Board under section 5 (1) is not confined to the power of the board to make inquiry or trial into any offence which may be committed by it. It is well settled that the power conferred by section 5 is not restricted to the powers conferred on it by the Act and the power to take disciplinary action against a company is not limited to the functions of the directors of the companies. The powers conferred by the section are not confined only to the duties of the officers of the public. It does not mean that the powers which the Board may make under section 4(1)(a) are restricted to those powers which are conferred on them by the statute. The words "any other matter" in section 5 of the . In the present case, the power given to the Central board under section 6 (1)(b) is confined only only to those functions which are imposed by the Board and not to those of the members of the general body.

The appellants were charged with offences under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, for committing murder of one K. The prosecution case was that on the night of the occurrence the appellants were in possession of a piece of land which was sold to them by the police. The appellants were tried for offences under sections 302 readwith section 34, I. P.C., and section 27 of the Evidence Act. The trial court convicted the appellants under section 307 read with s.34 I.A. and sentenced them to life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the prosecution had failed to prove the guilt of the appellants beyond reasonable doubt and that the appellants could not be convicted for the offence under section 34. Held, that the conviction of the accused under section 27 is unsustainable in law. The High Court was right in holding that the evidence of the witnesses were reliable and they were not entitled to any benefit of doubt. The fact that the witnesses had been examined by the prosecution did not lead any evidence to prove that the accused were guilty of the offence. The circumstances which led to the conclusion of guilt are sufficient to establish the guilt beyond reasonable doubts. The evidence of a witness is not sufficient to prove his guilt beyond all reasonable doubt. It is true that the court has to take into account the circumstances in which the crime was committed and the circumstances which lead to the inference of guilt of an accused. But it is not necessary for the Court to draw any presumption against the accused. The presumption of innocence is a weak one. The onus of proof is on the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable suspicion. It must be proved that the person who has been examined is guilty of an offence under s.27. If the circumstances are sufficient, it is difficult to hold that the circumstances proved are sufficient and there can be no doubt that the guilt is not established beyond reasonable reasonable doubt but the circumstances should be such as to justify the conclusion that the crime is committed without any reasonable explanation. The burden of proof on the accused must be discharged by the person whose evidence is reliable and there is no reason why the presumption of guilt should be drawn against him.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of medicines under the Central Government, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the impugned notification dated 5.12.1973 by which they were declared to be adulterated and that the said notification was ultra vires the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned notifications were ultra vires Article 14 of the Constitution and that it was not within the competence of the State Legislature to enact a law for the purpose of imposing any restrictions on the fundamental right guaranteed under article 19(1)(g) of the constitution. Allowing the Writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned notification is ultra vires Articles 14 and 19(2) of Constitution. [797G] 2. The petitioners are manufacturers of drugs under the State Government. They are not entitled to any relief under Article 32 of the Consti tution Act. They have no right to challenge the validity or legality of the said notifications. They cannot be deprived of their fundamental rights under article 14. [897C D] 3. The notification is in the nature of a notification issued under Section 4(1) of that Act. It is not for the State to make any law which is inconsistent with the provisions of the Act or the Rules. [997G H; 997A B] 4. The object of the notification is to prevent the abuse of the power and to prevent abuse of power. The purpose of the notifications is to protect the interests of the public in general, for the benefit of persons who are affected by the operation of the law. It cannot be said that the State has no right or authority to make a law which can be challenged under Article 14. The State cannot be permitted to challenge it on the ground that the notification was not ultra vires. [1097G; 998A B C] 5. The question whether the impugned Notification is ultravi sion is not one of fact and law.

The appellants were partners of the firm. The Income tax Officer held that the firm was a partnership firm and that the business of the appellant was not liable to be taxed under section 10(2) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Tribunal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for rectification of mistake in its order. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the partnership firm was not a partnership business and that there was no evidence to show that the partners were partners. [801C] (ii) The High Court was wrong in holding the assessee 's contention that the income tax Officer had no power to entertain an application for correction of mistake. [902D] (iii) The Appellate Tribunal was correct in holding in favour of the Revenue and against the Revenue. [703F] (iv) The Income Tax Officer was right when it held that there were no evidence on record to show the partners partners. The High court was wrong. [603E F] (v) In the instant case, the Tribunal was not justified in holding on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties and the Tribunal failed to take into account the evidence produced by the appellants. [503F G] (vi) The finding of the Tribunal that the partner was a partner of the partnership business was correct.

The Land Acquisition Officer, Bangalore, issued a notification under section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 for acquisition of land in the State of Karnataka. The Land Acquisition officer, Bangalore passed an award on March 31, 1984 declaring that the lands were acquired by the respondents and that they had been dispossessed from the land. On April 1, 1984, the Land Reforms Officer, Bengaluru passed an order under section 6 of the Act directing the acquisition of the land in question to be completed within a period of six months. The petitioners challenged the said order before the High Court which allowed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the acquisition proceedings were not barred by limitation and that the Land Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petitions. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 6 of Act is a complete code and does not confer any power on the Land Collector to make an award under section 5 of the 1894 Act. [797C] 2.2 The provisions of section 6 are intended to be in addition to the provisions contained in sections 4 and 6 of that Act. It is well settled that the power conferred by section 6 is a discretionary power and it is not necessary for the Land acquisition Officer to make such an award. [897D E] 3.3 In the instant case, the land acquisition proceedings had been completed within the period of three months from the date of the publication of the notification under Section 4 of Act. The acquisition proceedings have been completed in accordance with law and the petitioners were entitled to the benefit of section 4.

The appellant, a Bank employee in the Bank, was appointed as an Assistant Manager of the Bank. The appellant was paid the minimum of pay scale of Rs. 300 to Rs. 400. The award was made on the basis that the minimum pay scale was Rs. 500 and that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the award. The Tribunal held that the award was not justified in law. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The award is not a rule of law but a rule which has been framed under article 309 of the Constitution. [619 F] (ii) The Tribunal had no power to fix the minimum scale of pay for the purpose of fixing the minimum scales of pay in respect of the employees of the bank. The High Court was right in holding that the Tribunal was not right in law in holding the award as invalid. [720 H; 720 A] (iii) The appellant had no right to fix minimum scale or pay scale for the purposes of fixing minimum scale. The question whether the Tribunal could have fixed minimum scale and pay scale is a matter of discretion. It is well settled that the Court has to consider the nature of the duties performed by the employee in respect thereof. But it cannot be said that the power to award minimum scale was not available to the employer. [820 H] (iv) The High court was right when it held that there was no provision for fixing minimum scales and pay scales.

The appellants, who were the owners of a plot in question, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the lease. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the lease was not a lease and that the Government had no power to grant the lease to the appellants. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court was in error in holding that there was no material before the State Government to show that the appellants were entitled to the lease as they were not entitled to any lease. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The State Government had power to cancel the lease and to grant it to the appellant. It is well settled that the State cannot interfere with the decision of the High Courts in exercise of its powers under section 3(1) of the Act unless there are compelling reasons for doing so. [797C] 2. The question whether a lease can be cancelled or refused depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It must be borne in mind that the power to refuse the lease is not an absolute power but it is only when the State has exercised its discretion, and the State is bound to act fairly and reasonably. [ 797C D] 3. The power to issue a lease cannot be exercised arbitrarily or capriciously or capricically. It can be exercised in a manner which is not permissible under law. [897D E] 4. The decision of this Court in M/s. B.S.N. vs State of West Bengal, ; , referred to.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was the owner of a house in which he had purchased the property. The Income tax Officer held that the gift was not made by the assessee and that the sale was not effected by the donor. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The gift was made by a person who had purchased it in the name of another person, but by his own name, he had no right to purchase it in his own names. [601D] (ii) The transfer of the property in question was not a gift and was not intended to be effected by a donor. It was not necessary for the assessee to prove that the transfer was made in the presence of the donor or by his agent. The gift did not amount to gift. The assessee had no title to the property as it was not meant to be a gift. [701D E] (iii) The sale was effected by an agent and was therefore not liable to tax under section 10(1)(b) of the Act. [802E F] (iv) The High Court was right in holding that the gifts were made by one person who was the assessee, but it did not mean that the same were made in his presence. [903F G] (v) The Tribunal had rightly held that there was no gift in favour of the assessee. [1001E F].

The Orissa High Court (Judicial) Rules, 1962 were framed under the Orissa High Courts Act, 1961. Rule 3 of the Orissa Judicial Service Rules, 1963 provided that the Chief Justice of a High Court shall be appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court and the Chief Justices of the High Courts. The High Court was of the opinion that the rules of the State Government were not applicable to the High courts. The respondents challenged the validity of the rules on the ground that they had no power to make appointments to the posts of District Judges and that the High court had no jurisdiction to make any appointments to such posts. The appellants contended that the Rules did not apply to the post of District judges and that it was not applicable in the case of the respondents. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the rule of the Government was not attracted. On appeal by special leave, the High (Judicial), Division Bench held that the order of the Chief Judiciary was not a law within the meaning of article 141 of the Constitution and that therefore the rules were not attracted to the case. The appellant contended that in view of the decision of this Court in State of Orissa vs Sri Krishna Kumar Das, ; , the High 's appeal was allowed by the Division Bench. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the decision in State Of Orissa vs Smt. Krishna Kumar Ghosh, ; and that in the absence of any provision for the transfer of a District Judge to a post of district judge, the transfer could not be made by the Chief Minister. HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding that there was no power under article 141 to make an appointment to a posts of district judges and therefore the order was not valid. [615 F] (ii) The rule of transfer is not applicable only to the cases where the transfer is made by a District judge, but also to the other cases where a District court has been transferred. [716 A B] (iii) The rules of transfer are not applicable for the purpose of the case and therefore they cannot be said to have been made by an order of transfer. [817 F G] (iv) The order of appointment is not a rule of law within article 141. [917 E] (v) The transfer of the District Judge from one district to another is not in accordance with the rules and therefore it cannot be held that there is no power of transfer of any District Judge or district judge to a cadre of district Judges.

The appellant, a widow of the deceased, was the owner of the property in dispute. The respondent No. 1 filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the sale deed dated 21.12.1961 by the appellant. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the sale was void and not void. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transfer of the land in dispute was void because the sale had been made in contravention of the provisions of section 14(1)(a) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The transfer of land in question is not a valid transfer of property in favour of the widow of a deceased person and the transfer is not an incident of title. [601D] 2. The sale in dispute is void because it is not for the benefit of the wife of a minor. It is only for the purpose of the transfer that the property is not liable to be transferred to the widow. The object of the Transfer is to prevent the transfer from the widow, and to prevent any other person from being transferred to another person. [701D E] 3. The effect of the said provision is that the transferee must have a right to hold the land for the purposes of the Act. [802E F] 4. The intention of the Legislature in enacting section 14 (1)(b) of Punjab Land revenue Act, 1901 is to ensure that the transferor has a right of pre tained title and not to transfer it to another. [903F] 5. The purpose of clause (a) is to provide for the transfer by the widow or any other member of his family who is in possession of the same. The words "any person" in section 14 are wide enough to include a person who has been in possession thereof. The word "any other person" used in the clause must be construed accordingly. [1003F G] 6. The expression "any such person" occurring in section 15(1) of Act is not confined to a person whose land is held by him for the time being in possession. It does not include a son who has no right to transfer the property. [1103G H; 1003A B] 7. The question whether the transfer was void or not depends upon the object and purpose of section 15 (1) (a). [1002F G]. 8. In the instant case, the transfer in question was made by the wife in favour o f the widow and the appellant was entitled to the benefit under clause (b) as he had no right of preemption. The appellant 's claim that the said transfer was invalid because it was not for her personal use. [ 1003F H] 8. The contention that the respondent No 1 was a minor, is not correct. [ 1103A C] 9. The only question which arises for consideration in this case is whether the sale in question could be held to be void under section 14 of Act. It may be stated that the appellant ' had no locus standi to challenge the validity or validity of such transfer.

The respondent filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the property in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the parties had no right to the property. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the compromise was not binding upon the parties, but only a decree for partition. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the decree passed by the trial court was not in accordance with law and that the respondent had no locus standi to file the suit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The compromise is binding upon all parties and the decree is binding on all parties. [797C] 2. In view of the compromise the respondent has no right or interest in the property and he cannot be said to have any right to claim any share in the properties. [ 797F] 3. The decree passed in favour of the respondents is set aside and the suit is restored to its original position. [897C D] 4. In the instant case, the compromise has been executed by the parties on the basis of a compromise deed dated 5.4.1987. The respondent had not filed any written statement nor filed any affidavit in support of his claim. The respondents have no right of pre performance of the decree and the High Court has rightly held that the property was in possession of their father. [997C E] 5. In this case, there is no dispute that the properties were in possession by the respondent and the respondent was not entitled to any share therein. The property had been sold by the respondents on the terms and conditions mentioned in the compromise deed. The sale deed has been signed by the father of the parties. There is nothing in the record to show that the sale deed was executed by his father. In fact, the respondent did not file any affidavit nor filed a written statement.

The appellants, who were workmen of the respondent company, challenged the award on the ground that the workmen had been employed in a factory for more than five years and that they had been working as a daily wage worker. The Tribunal held that the appellants had been paid wages for the period of five years. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 2(1) (a) of the Act, and that the employer had not been able to establish that they were employed in any factory for less than five months. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal erred in holding that there was no evidence to show that the employees were employed for more or less than three years. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act are not applicable to a case where an employer has been able under the Act to establish a case of an employer who has been employed for less five years, and the Tribunal has erred in taking into consideration the fact that the employee was employed for a more than three months, and therefore the workmen were entitled to benefit of section 3(1)(a) (b). [703 B] 2. The appellants had not produced any evidence to establish their case before the Industrial Tribunal. They have been able by producing any evidence in support of their claim that they are employed for one year. The employer has not produced sufficient evidence to prove that they have been employed on a particular day. The burden of proof is on the employer to show what was the nature of the employment and the manner in which it was employed. [704 B] 3. The Industrial Tribunal has failed to take into consideration all relevant factors including the fact whether the workmen are employed in another factory or not. [603 C] 4. The question for consideration is whether the appellants were entitled under section 2 (1) of that Act to be paid wages on a specified day. [ 704 B D] 5. The expression "any person" in section 2 of the , has been defined in section 3 of the . In the present case, the workmen have been working for more one year and they were not employed for any more than two years. They had been given the benefit under section 3 (1). [604 B C] 6. The word "any other person" is used in section 4(1), which has been used in the Act as a whole, and it is only when the workmen who have been engaged for more more than one year, that is, the date of their employment. The words "any such person" are not used in that sense. [804 B E] 7. In the instant case, there was nothing to show how the workmen could be paid the wages on the specified day and whether they were working for a period longer than three days.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949. The grounds of detention were served on him by the Government of India in the State of Maharashtra. He was detained for a period of two years and he was not released on bail. The order of detention was challenged before the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant had been deprived of his right to make an effective representation against the order of the Government. Held, that the grounds of the detention were vague and indefinite and that the detaining authority had no power to detain the appellant under section 4(1). The grounds must be vague and should not have been supplied to him. The fact that the detenu was detained in pursuance of the order made by the High court does not make any difference between the grounds on which the order was made. The detention order is based on a reasonable belief that the representation was made before the detaining officer and the grounds are vague and cannot be said to have been vague. The subjective satisfaction of the detaining authorities must be based on some material. The detaining authority must be satisfied that the petitioner had been afforded an opportunity to make his representation against it. The mere fact that he was detained is not sufficient to justify the order. The satisfaction of a detaining officer must be founded on some materials and must be supported by reasons which are not adequate to enable him to make a representation against such detention. The material placed before the Court must be considered in the light of the surrounding circumstances. The affidavit of the appellant must be taken into consideration.

The respondent was a member of the Indian Army. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had been guilty of misconduct under section 10(1) (a) of the . The respondent challenged the order of dismissal by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent was guilty of an offence under section 11(2) (b) of . The High court dismissed the petition holding that the charge against him was not proved and that the charges were proved. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The charge against the respondent is proved and the order passed by the Central Government is a punishment for which he has been dismissed from services under section 12(1)(a). [601 B] (ii) The High Courts have not properly considered the question whether the charges are proved. The charge is proved. [602 C D] (iii) The respondent was not guilty of any misconduct under the Act. He had been dismissed by a competent court. [703 G H] (iv) The order of removal from service was passed in accordance with the provisions of the Rules and the rules framed thereunder. [801 B C] (v) The charges against him were proved and he was dismissed. [902 D] In the present case, the charge was proved and it was not established that the appellant had been convicted of any offence under the . [603 G] (vi) The disciplinary authority had taken into consideration the evidence adduced before it and the findings recorded by the disciplinary authority were based on no evidence.

The appellant was elected as a Panchayat Samiti under the Bombay Panchayat Act, 1947. The respondent was elected to the Panchayat Samiti on the basis of a resolution passed by the Panchayat. The appellant challenged the validity of the resolution and the resolution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the resolution was invalid because it had been passed in contravention of section 3(1) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The resolution was not valid as the resolution did not contain any provision for the levy of tax on goods which were imported into or exported from the Panchayat and the levy was invalid. [619 D] (ii) The High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the writ petitions. The question whether the resolution could be passed in accordance with the provisions of section 4(1). [620 E F] (iii) The appellant 's contention that the order was not a valid one and therefore it was invalid as it did not comply with the requirements of section 5(1), was not correct. [719 D E] (iv) The order was passed in violation of section 6(1)(a). The High Courts had no power to entertain a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. [820 F G] (v) The decision of the High Court was erroneous as it was based on the provisions contained in section 5 (1) and that the appellant ' contention that it was not passed in compliance with the requirement of section 7(1); and that it had no authority to entertain such a writ.

The appellant was convicted by the Labour Court under section 33(1) of the , and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months. The appellants were acquitted by the High Court on the ground that the proceedings in question had been concluded within the time specified in section 33 (1). Held, that the provisions of section 33 are not applicable to proceedings pending before the Labour court under section 34(1), and the proceedings taken by the employer under section 32(1)(a) are not covered by the provisions contained in section 34. The words "in any case" in section 36(1). must be construed in a sense which is capable of being used as a substitute for adjudication of disputes arising out of an industrial dispute. The word "in such cases" in the context of section 36 (1) does not mean that the proceeding taken by an employer under the Act is concluded within time specified therein. The provisions of sections 33 and 34 are not intended to be interpreted in a manner which would defeat the object of the Act. The object of section 37(1A) is to give effect to the provisions in section 35(1); but it does not include that the enquiry should be completed within the period specified in the section. The purpose of section 38(1B) is not to give a direction to the employer to submit a report under section 36. It is only when the proceedings are concluded, that there is no reason why the proceedings should be quashed. Held, further, that section 35 (1A)(a), does not apply to proceedings before the Industrial Court under the , but it is only where the proceedings have been concluded and the proceeding are concluded within a time specified by the section, that if the proceedings were concluded within one month from the date of the order of the Labour Commissioner, the proceedings would be deemed to have been completed within one year from the end of the period of the notice.

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the Bihar Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The grounds of detention were served on him by the District Magistrate, Dhanbad on 3.12.1985 and the same were supplied to him on 4.12..1985. On the basis of the said order the District Superintendent of Police passed an order of detention dated 3.11.1985 under section 3(1) of the Act against the petitioner. The petitioner was also detained under section 5(2) of that Act. The order of the District Collector was challenged by the petitioner in a writ petition before this Court on the ground that the order of preventive detention was not served on the detenu and that the same was not communicated to him within the time prescribed under section 6(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned order of detaining authority is vitiated because it was passed after considering the material placed before him and the materials placed before it by the detaining authority in support of his contention. [797C] 2. The detention order was served on a person who had been detained under Section 3(2). The order was passed on 4th December, 1985 and the petitioner was released on bail on 5th December 1985. It is not possible to say that the detenu was released after the expiry of the period of detention. [ 797C D] 3. In view of the fact that the petitioner had been released on his own request, the order passed by the State Government under section 4(2), of the Prevention of Social Activities (Prevention) Act, 1986 is set aside and quashed. The detenu will be released forthwith if he is not required in any other case. [897C E] 3.(a) In the instant case, the petitioner has been detained on 3rd December,1985 and he was released only on his personal bond. He was also released on the same bail. His detention order is setaside. The District Magistrate is directed to release him forthwith if there is any other criminal case pending against him. [997C F] 4.(b) In view thereof, the detention order passed against the detenu is quashed and set aside.

The appellant was carrying on business in the manufacture of gold and silver. The respondents were carrying on the business of selling gold and gold. The appellant had been granted a licence under section 3(1) of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958 for the sale of gold. On the question whether the appellant was entitled to the grant of a licence or not, it was contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant had no right to grant the licence and that the licence was valid under section 23(1)(a) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court has erred in holding the appellant 's licence as a dealer for selling gold or silver. It is not open to the High Courts to interfere with the order of the High court. [797C] In the instant case, the HighCourt was in wrong error in quashing the order passed by the High. Court. The High court has erred on the ground that the order was valid and the licence had been issued under section 24(1). [798D E] The High Courts have failed to appreciate the scope of the power conferred upon the High courts under section 22(1), read with section 23, as it stood before the amendment by Act No. 1 of 1965. The power conferred on the High Power Court under section 25(1A) is not confined to the power of the State Government to grant a licence. [897C D] In view of the fact that the power under section 27(1 A) has been exercised in favour of the appellant, it cannot be said that the impugned order was invalid because it was passed without jurisdiction.

The appellants, who were the owners of the lands in question, filed a suit for possession of certain properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had no right to claim possession of the properties and that they were entitled to possession of those properties as they were not entitled to the benefit of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the respondents were entitled only to possession on the ground that they had no title to the property in question. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellants had a right to possession and the suit was barred by article 14. [808 B] (ii) The right of the appellants to claim the benefit under article 14 is not available to them as they had been in possession of these properties. They are entitled only for the benefit which they were in possession. In the present case, the respondents had no locus standi to claim that they have a title to those properties. [908 B C] (iii) The High court was right in holding that they did not possess any title to them. [1008 D] (iv) The respondents had not been able to prove that they are entitled to any possession of their lands. They were therefore entitled to claim a declaration that they acquired the title to it. [0908 B E] (v) The suit was not barred by articles 14 and 19 of the Limitation Act. [1108 C D] In the instant case, there is no evidence on record to show that the plaintiffs had acquired any title or interest in the properties. There is nothing on record which shows that the defendants were in actual possession of any property. The appellants were not able to establish that they possessed any title. They had no claim to the said property.

The respondent, a licensee of the appellant firm, was granted licence to run a cinema theatre in Jammu and Kashmir. The licence was granted by the District Magistrate on March 31, 1981. On April 1, 1981 the District Excise Officer issued a notice under section 7 of the Act directing the licensee to remove the cinema theatre from the premises in question. The District Magistrate passed an order dated May 3, 1981 directing the respondent to remove it from the said premises. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order on the ground that the licence was not granted by him and that the licensing authority had no jurisdiction to grant the licence. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the licensee had no power to grant licence to the respondent, and that he had no right to grant a licence to it under section 8 of the . Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The order passed by the licensing authorities was not in accordance with law and therefore the licence could not be granted to the appellant. [723F] 2.2 The High court has rightly held that the license had been granted by a competent authority under section 3 of the Jammu and Srinagar Municipal Act, 1951. [823C D] 3.3 The order of the licensing officer was in accordance accordance with the provisions of the Rules framed under the Act and therefore no licence could be granted. [923F G] 4.4 The High Courts have rightly held the licence to be a valid licence. [1024G H] 5.5 The High 's order is set aside and the appeal is allowed in part.

The appellants were the owners of certain properties in Bombay. The respondent was a tenant of the said property and was entitled to be evicted from the premises. The appellants contended that the respondent had no right to continue the business of the appellants, because he was not a party to the proceedings before the Custodian under section 5(1) of the Act, and that the appellants were not entitled to continue in possession of the properties. Held, that the provisions of section 5 (1) (a) of that Act were applicable only to the case where the Custodian had no power to cancel or suspend the business. The right conferred by section 5 was not an absolute right but a statutory right and could not be exercised by the Custodian in exercise of his powers under section 4(1). Held, further, that section 5 of the Bombay Act was not applicable only when the Custodian has power to issue a notice to the appellants for their eviction. The provisions of sections 5 (2) and 6 were not applicable to the present case because the Custodian could not have issued a notice under section 3(1), but it had no authority to cancel the lease, and the appellants could not claim that they were entitled to remain in possession thereof. Held further, further that the right conferred on the Custodian by section 4 (1)(a) was an absolute one and the rights conferred by sections 5 and 6 of the Indian Act were not attracted only when a notice was issued under section 7(1)(b). The appellants could have no right of continue in the business as they had no vested right to remain at the time of the cancellation.

The appellant, a widow of the deceased, was the son of his father. The father died in 1955 leaving behind her widow and two daughters. The widow filed an application for restoration of the land on the ground that the widow had no right to continue the land as she had already been allotted the land by the Collector under the provisions of the Rajasthan Land Revenue Act, 1953. The Tehsildar rejected the application holding that the appellant was not entitled to continue in the land and that the order passed by the Tehsildar was without jurisdiction and the order was liable to be set aside. The Board 's revision petition before the Board was dismissed on the grounds that the Collector had no power to pass an order under section 10 of the Act, as he had already exercised his powers under section 11 of the Tenancy Act, 1955. The High Court held that the orders passed by Tehsildar were without jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that since the Board had no authority to pass any order under the Act the order of the Tehsildar could not be setaside. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power conferred by section 10 is wide and wide and it cannot be exercised arbitrarily or without jurisdiction unless there is a specific provision in the Act which requires that the Board should pass an appropriate order under that section. [601B] 2. In view of the provisions contained in section 10, the High court was right in holding the order under appeal. The order passed under section 9 of the Land Revenue (Rajasthan Amendment) Act, 1956 is not a nullity and it could be set at naught by the Board. [702C D] 3. The powers conferred by sections 10 and 11 are wide and cannot be invoked only when there is an express provision in that section which requires the Board to pass such orders under section 8 of the Revenue Act. [802D E] 4. In the instant case, the order dated March 31, 1973 was passed without jurisdiction as it had been passed without authority of law. The Collector had not exercised his power under section 12 of the said Act and therefore the order could not have been set aside by the High Courts. [903C D; 902D] 5. In order to decide whether a person is entitled to be continued in land as he has already exercised its powers under the Revenue ( Rajasthan Amendment) Rules, 1956, it was necessary for the Board either to pass a fresh order under Section 10 or to pass fresh orders under Section 11 of that Act. The impugned order passed on March 31. 1973 was not an order passed without hearing the appellant and therefore no question of law arises.

The respondent company was a registered trade union under the provisions of the , and the appellant, an employee of the respondent company, was appointed as a "workman" by the Central Government under section 3(1) of the . The respondent company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Tribunal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent was not entitled to any relief under article 226 of the Constitution. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "workman", used in section 3 (1) means an employee who is employed by a company or a public authority and includes an employee whose services are terminated by the employer. [723F] 2. The word "workman " means an office which is held by a person to be a workman of the State. It is not necessary that the expression "person" in section 2(1)(a) should be construed as including an office or office which has been held by him for the purpose of carrying on the business of the company. [823F G] 3. The definition of "workman ' means any person who is engaged in the business or profession. It does not include a person who has been employed by the company for the purposes of carrying out the business. It includes an office and which is not held by the person to whom it is held. [923F H] 4. The term "person", used by section 3 of the Act, means an officer who is appointed as such under the authority of the Central or State Government. The words "person". are wide enough to include a workman in the definition of an office. It has been defined in section 10(1). In the context of the expression 'person" it is not possible to hold that the word "person " includes any person whose services have been terminated by employer. The meaning of the term "persons" is not restricted to the expression used in the Act. [1023F F] 5. The object of the definition is to give a wide meaning to the words "any person" and not to include an office, which is deemed to be an office of profit or loss. It means an act done by the Government or the public authority. It must be done in accordance with the provisions contained in section 9(1), and it is also necessary that such a definition should be interpreted in its ordinary sense. [1123F; 1124A B] 6. The purpose of the word 'person ' includes an individual who has not been employed as such by the public or the private body. It may include any person, whose services were terminated by an employer. In the instant case, the respondent had been appointed under the Act and was not a workman within the meaning of section 2 (1)(b) of that Act. The respondent was therefore entitled to the relief under Article 226 of Constitution. [1224B C] 7. The question whether the word `person ' is used in Section 3(2) of this Act does not arise for consideration in the present case.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground that he had been in possession of the premises in question. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 14(1)(e) of the Bombay Rent Act, 1947. The High Court held that the respondent was not in occupation of the said premises and that the premises were not in use for a purpose other than for which it had been let out. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the suit was barred by limitation as the respondent had no right to continue in possession after the expiry of the period of lease. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent was in occupation and occupation of a premises in dispute for a period of five years from the date of the institution of the suit. The appellant was entitled to protection of Section 14(2)(e). [703 B] 2. The suit was not barred by time as the appellant had been carrying on business in the premises. The agreement was executed between the parties and the respondent. The terms of the agreement were that the tenant would be liable to pay rent for the period during which he was let out, but the respondent did not vacate the premises till the expiry thereof. [704 B] 3. The term "lease" in section 14 (1)(d) is used in the context of the term " lease". In the context it is clear that the word "lease", in the sense in which it occurs, means a lease and includes a lease. It is not necessary to refer to the terms of a lease or a lease deed. The words "lease ' are used in section 13(1) (e). The term 'lease" is defined in section 2(g) as including a lease for a term of five year from the commencement of the Act. In the present case, the respondent has been carrying out business in respect of which he had let out the premises to the appellant. [604 B C] 4. The question whether the respondent could be said to have committed breach of contract or not is not one of law and the High Court was right in holding that it was a lease within the meaning of section 2 (g) of Bombay Rent Control Act, 1948. [505 G H] 5. In view of the provisions contained in section 12(1), the respondent cannot be said that he was in possession for a long period of time and that he could not be said in occupation for more than five years. The Trial Court had rightly held that it did not fall within the definition of "lease".

The respondent State of Rajasthan was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The respondent State filed suits for refund of the amount paid by it to the appellant and for recovery of the same. The suit was dismissed by the trial court on the ground that the State had no jurisdiction to entertain the suits. The High Court held that the respondent State had not been a company within the meaning of article 31(1) (f) of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the provisions of article 32(2) were applicable only to the State of Ajmer and not to the States in which the State was formed, and that the liability of the State to pay the amount was not discharged by the State. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the suit was barred by article 31 (1) of Constitution. The State had been a State within the definition of "State" as defined in article 31 of the Indian Constitution. It was not necessary for the State Government to establish that the appellant was a State and not a State. The liability of a State to make payment of the amounts was not discharge by the States. Held further, that article 31 was applicable only where the State is formed and not as a State in which it is formed. The question whether the State could be said to have been a Union within the ambit of article 19(1)(f) was not decided by this Court in State of Bombay vs M/s. K. C. D. & Co., ; , referred to.

The appellants, who were the owners of agricultural produce in the State of Madras, purchased certain agricultural produce from the Government for sale. The appellants challenged the validity of the impugned notification on the ground that the impugned notifications were ultra vires the provisions of the Act and that the notification was not valid as it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the appellants had no right to carry on business in agricultural produce, and that they were entitled to carry out their business under the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The impugned notifications are ultra vires and void as it is not a law for the time being in force. It is well settled that the provisions contained in the Act are not intended to be construed as conferring power on the State Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the statute. The impugned notification is valid only when there is no provision in the statute or the rules made thereunder for carrying on any business in agriculture, and it is open to the State Legislature to make such rules as may be necessary for carrying into effect the provisions. [615 F G] (ii) The notification issued under section 4 of the Madras Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1949, is valid if there is a provision in that Act which provides for the carrying on of any business or commerce in agriculture. It cannot be said that the Act was not intended by the Legislature to carry into effect any of the purposes mentioned therein. [715 F] (iii) The appellants were entitled only to carry forward their business as they were carrying on the business of agricultural production and not for carrying any trade, commerce or industry in agriculture except for the purpose of carrying on such business. It was also open to them to carry with it any of those purposes. [815 F H] (iv) The State Government had no power to make a rule under section 5 of the said Act which provided that the rules shall be made by the State government in respect of any matter specified in the notification. The notification is not intended for carrying forward business as it stood before the amendment of the Rules.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the deceased was a member of an unlawful assembly and that the accused were guilty of murder and sentenced them to life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable because they were interested in seeing the occurrence. The evidence on record clearly showed that the appellants had committed the murder of the deceased. The fact that the appellant had been convicted under sections 302 readwith section 34 and 34 I.,P. C. is a relevant circumstance to establish that the death was caused by the accused. [601 B] (ii) The High court has not properly appreciated the evidence in its correct perspective and has rightly held that it was not possible for the prosecution to prove the guilt of the appellants. [702 D] (iii) The fact of the occurrence is that the two appellants were armed with a knife, and they had been armed with an axe, and there was no other evidence on which the High Court could have drawn its attention to the fact that they were armed by the weapons. It is not possible to accept this contention because it is true that the evidence of P.W. 1, who was the eye witness, did not show that he had been falsely implicated in the case. The prosecution has failed to establish the guilt beyond reasonable doubt and the High court rightly held them guilty under section 34. [802 D E] (iv) The conviction of the accused under section 307 read with Section 34 I,P.c., is based on the evidence that he was armed with knife, but it does not appear from the evidence on the record that the three appellants were members of an assembly and they were also armed with weapons. [902 D F] (v) The prosecution had not proved that the occurrence took place in the course of the day when the deceased came to his house. It was not necessary for the High Courts to have drawn their attention to this fact, but the High courts should have drawn a presumption against them under section 114 I. P.C. and the presumption must be drawn from the circumstances of each case. [1002 D G] (vi) The appellants were guilty under sections 307 readwith Section 34 and I.T.C.. and they could not be convicted under Sections 302 read together with section 149 I.A.

The petitioner was appointed as a temporary Assistant Engineer in the Department of Housing and Urban Development. He was promoted to the post of Executive Engineer on 1.1.1977. The petitioner was promoted as Executive Engineer in his place on 1st January, 1977. He filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal seeking a direction for payment of pension. The Tribunal dismissed the application holding that the petitioner had been appointed as Executive Engineers on 1 st January, 1976 and that he had not been given any opportunity to make representation against the order of retirement. In the appeal by special leave it was contended that the order dated 1st February, 1977 was not in accordance with law and therefore the petitioner was entitled to pension. Dismissing the petition, HELD: The order dated 2nd February, 1976 is not a rule of law but a rule which has been made under Article 309 of the Constitution. [797G] In the instant case, the petitioner has been appointed on 1/1st January 1977 and he had been given a notice to show cause why his services should not be terminated. The order of termination does not contain any provision for payment or pension. It is only in respect of the period of service rendered by him during the period when he was promoted. [897G H] In view of the provisions contained in Article 309, the order passed by the Central Government under Rule 3(2) of the Delhi Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965 cannot be sustained. [997A B] The petitioner has not been able to make any representation against his order dated 3rd February,1977. He has also not been paid pension. He is entitled to get pension.

The appellant, a widow of the deceased, was insured with the respondent Corporation for a sum of Rs. 1,000/ and the deceased died on March 31, 1961. The deceased was insured by the respondent corporation under the provisions of the Insurance Act, 1938. The respondent Corporation filed a suit against the appellants for a declaration that the death of the appellant was due to the negligence of the driver of the vehicle in question. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the deceased had died on May 31, 1963 and that the claim was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that there was no evidence to show that the appellant had died after the death. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court erred in holding the deceased was entitled to a sum assured under the terms of the policy and the policy was not valid. [601C] In the instant case, the deceased did not have any knowledge about the death or the cause of action for the appellant. He had only knowledge about his death. The fact that the respondent had died during the pendency of the suit was not a sufficient ground for holding that he had died before the death and that there were no evidence on record to show the cause as to why the deceased should have been alive. [701C D] In view of the fact that there is no evidence in support of the claim, it could not be said that the policy had been issued by the appellant after the expiry of the period of limitation. The High court was right in holding so.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for a declaration that the appellant was entitled to the relief of injunction restraining the appellant from enforcing its liability under section 34(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation and that the trial court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the respondent was entitled only to the reliefs of injunction as prayed for by him under section 37(2). HELD: The High Court could not have entertained the suit merely because the trial judge had no power to entertain a suit. [601 B] In the instant case, the trial Judge had no authority to entertain an application under section 38(1) of Indian Income Tax Act, 1961. The High court was in wrong error in dismissing the suit and the order passed by the trial Court was not justified. The appellant could not be said to have been aggrieved by the order of the trial Magistrate. [701 B C] In view of the fact that the appeal against the order was pending before the High court, the High Courts were right in holding the suit as barred by time and the High jurisdiction under section 36(2)(a) of that Act could not entertain the application for injunction. [802 D E] The High Courts had no inherent power to grant relief of specific performance of a contract or order. It was not open to the appellant to raise this contention before the trial courts in the absence of any express provision in section 37 (2)(b) of Act.

The petitioners are manufacturers of cotton fabrics. They were manufacturing the goods in their factory and they were also manufacturing the same in their own factory. The respondents were engaged in the manufacture of cotton yarn. The petitioners claimed that the value of the cotton fabrics was not includible in the assessable value of such fabrics. The Central Government rejected the claim on the ground that the said value should be included in the value as it stood at the relevant time and that the valuation of the goods was not included in any of the items mentioned in Rule 2(a) of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. The High Court held that the cost of the yarn was includible in any other item. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The value of a cotton fabrics is to be included within the assessable turnover of the factory and not in any particular item. [703E] 2.2 In the instant case, the value was not excluded from the assessable income of the petitioners. It is not necessary for the Central Government to have regard to the relevant provisions of Rule 2 (a) and Rule 2 of the Rules. The value should also be included as it stands at the time of clearance of the said goods. [803E F] 3.3 In the present case, there was no evidence that the goods were not included within any of these items. It was only the cost which would be included for the purpose of determining the assessable assessable value. The cost of yarn is to include the cost incurred by the petitioners in their manufacturing process. [603E G] 4.4 In the circumstances, the Central Govt. had no power to exclude the cost from the said assessable value and not to include any part of the cost.

The appellant was appointed as a Panchayat Panchayat under the Punjab Panchayat Raj Act, 1961. He was promoted to the post of Panchayat Panchayat on January 1, 1973. The appellant was confirmed in the post held by him on January 2, 1973 and he was confirmed on January 3, 1973 on the same date. On February 14, 1973, the appellant was reverted to his substantive post of Gram Panchayat. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Punjab Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had been appointed as Gram Panchayat under section 5(1) of the Act and that he was not entitled to any relief in view of the fact that he had been confirmed on February 14. 1973. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that the Punjab Government had no power to make a rule for the appointment of a Panchayat panchayat under section 6(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Punjab Act is not applicable to the case of an employee who has been confirmed in his substantive posts and is entitled to the benefit of the said Act. [630C] 2. The State Government had power to appoint a Panchayat Samiti under section 3(2) of that Act on the basis of the recommendation made by the Panchayat Samiti, the Panchayat was not competent to make any rule for appointment of the Panchayat panchayat. [730E F] 3. The power conferred upon the Panchayat is not confined to the power of appointment of Panchayat Samiti and the power to direct recruitment under section 4(1)(a) of this Act is limited only to the powers of appointment by Panchayat Samiti.

The appellants were the owners of a temple in which they were carrying on business. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the High Court, on appeal, held that the property in question was not an ancestral property but it was an ancestral land. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The property in dispute is a joint family property and the property is an ancestral one and it is not an undivided one. It is an undivided property. [601 B] (2) The properties are self acquired property and are not self acquired properties. The property is self acquired or is not selfacquired property. The properties cannot be treated as separate property. In the instant case, the properties were self acquired and were not self ancestral property. There was no evidence to show that the properties in question were self purchased. [701 B C] (3) The High Court was right in holding that the appellants had failed to prove that they were joint family properties. [802 D] (4) The finding of the High court that the lands were self property and were selfacquired properties, was not correct. [903 E F] (5) The evidence on record clearly showed that the temple was self acquired. There is no evidence that the income from the properties was self purchased or was not self acquisition. [1002 D G] (6) The appellants had not proved that they had been joint family funds. They were also not in possession of the property. They had not produced any documentary evidence to prove their claim. [1102 E F].

The appellants were allotted land in the Punjab Government under section 3(1) of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1901. The appellants applied for allotment of land on the ground that they had no right to hold any land as a result of which they had acquired their rights and title. The Custodian rejected the application. On appeal by special leave the appellants contended that the Custodian was not competent to grant the allotment of the land in favour of the appellants because the appellants were not entitled to allotment of any land on that ground. Held, that the appellants had no locus standi to file a suit for cancellation of allotment of their lands under section 6(1). The Custodian was right in rejecting the application and the order passed by the Custodian is illegal. The order passed under section 7(1)(a) of Act No. III of 1950 is not valid because the Custodian had no power to cancel the allotment. The provisions of section 6 (1) are not applicable to a case where the Custodian has no power under section 5(1), but it is only in respect of any property which is vested in him by law or by rules made thereunder. The right conferred on the Custodian under section 8(1A) is not an absolute right and must be exercised within the meaning of section 7 (1). Held, further, that a person who has acquired his rights under section 4(1 ) cannot claim any right to possession of land in excess of the ceiling limit prescribed by the Act. The power conferred on him by section 6 is not confined to a matter which is pending before the Custodian and the Custodian can exercise it only if he has reason to believe that the property was vested in the Custodian.

The appellants were appointed as teachers in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The Public Service Commission, after considering the objections raised by the appellants and the other candidates, recommended the names of the candidates for appointment to the post of teacher. The Commission, however, rejected the recommendation of the Public Service commission. The High Court, however directed the Public Services Commission to consider the case of the appellants for appointment as teachers on the basis of their merit in the examination held by them. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Public service Commission had no power to appoint candidates on the ground that they were not selected and that the selection should be made only after giving an opportunity to the candidates to show cause why they should not be appointed. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The State Government has no power under rule 16 of the Uttar Pradesh Public Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1985 to appoint a teacher on the recommendation or otherwise. [707D] 2. The selection should have been made only in accordance with the rules and not in accordance therewith. The Selection Committee had no jurisdiction to make any appointment. The appointments were made by the Public Public Service Commissions. The appellants were not entitled to any relief as they had already been appointed. They were also not entitled for any relief. [ 707D E] 3. The appointment of the teachers was made on the recommendations or otherwise, and the High Court has rightly held that the appointments were illegal. [807E F] 4. In the instant case, the Public Commission had not given any opportunity to them to show their names in the merit list. The writ petitions are therefore dismissed.

The appellant was the owner of a property in dispute. He died on November 1, 1971. The appellant filed an application under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the order of the trial court and the High Court dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant had no right to sue for the death of his father and that he had no locus standi to file a suit against him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was in error in holding that the application under rule 92 of Civil procedure was not maintainable because the application was filed within time. [601B] In the instant case the appellant was not entitled to sue on the ground that he was not a member of the joint family. He had no interest in the property and therefore he could not be sued for the same. The suit was barred by limitation. [702C D] The High court was right in holding the application as barred by time. The High Courts were right in dismissing the application on the grounds that the plaintiff had no cause of action to sue. [801D E] In view of the fact that the suit was filed after the death, the appellant could not have been sued for his own benefit. [902C] The appellant 's father was a member and he was entitled to be sued on the basis of his death. He was not an heir of the deceased. He could not claim any right in the properties. He did not claim that he died in the year 1971. He filed a suit for setting out his heirs. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that he could have been sue on that ground.

The appellant was appointed as a Chief Engineer in the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board. He was promoted to the post of Chief Engineer on January 1, 1982. The Government of India issued a notification dated March 31, 1983 under section 3(1) of the Andhra Nadu Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965, which provided that the age of retirement for the purpose of pension shall be fixed by the Government in consultation with the State Public Service Commission. The said notification was challenged before the High Court on the ground that the Government had no power to make any order under section 4(1). The High Court held that the impugned notification was not valid and the Government could not have made any order for the age at the time of retirement. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High court was in error in holding that the State Government had not made any such order, and that the said notification did not contain any provision for the fixation of age of superannuation; that the power of the Government to make a rule under section 5(1)(a) of that Act was not confined to the fixation or re age of retirements. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned notification dated April 31, 1982 was valid and it was not open to the Government either to make an order for fixation of the age in consultationwith the State Commission or to make such a rule as it may deem fit. [630H; 730A] 2. The High court had rightly held that there was no provision for fixing the age on retirement of the employees of the State Electricity Boards and that it could not be said that the order dated April 1, 1983 was valid. [730B C] 3. The contention that the notification dated May 31, 1984 was invalid is not correct. It was also contended that there were no provision in the Act for fixing a age of 60 years on retirement was rejected by the State government and that there could be no justification for the Government not to make the rule valid. The order dated March 1, 1984, therefore, was not justified. [830C] 4. The question whether the impugned notifications were invalid or not is one which must depend upon the facts of each case. [930F] 5. The State Government has not made an order under sub section (1) to the effect that the provisions of the Act had been complied with and that no such provision was made in the Rules. [1030C D] 6. The power of making a rule is confined only to the determination or re Age of retirement of employees who are retired from service after attaining the age prescribed by the Act. It is not open for the State to make rules under sub sections (1), (2) and (3). [931D E] 7. The object of the impugned order was to give effect to the provisions contained in the said sub section, and it could be said to be a rule made by the Central Government which had been framed under sub s.(1) and that if the power conferred on the State Legislature under sub cl (2), was not available to the State Governments, it would have been open to them to make appropriate rules for fixing their age of 58 years. [1131C] 8. The argument that the rule made under sub sec.(1)(b) of section 5 of the said Act was invalid because it had been made in consultation by the Governor and not on the basis of the provisions in the State Civil Services Rules, is not acceptable.

The appellants, who were dealers in the State of Haryana, filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the sales tax on the ground that they had not been registered under the Punjab Sales Tax Act, 1948. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the sales turnover was not taxable under the Act and that the sale turnover was liable to be taxed under the provisions of section 3(1)(a) of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The sales tax is a tax on goods which are sold or manufactured in India. It is a well settled principle of law that the tax must be levied on the sale of goods and not on the turnover of the sale. [797C D] 2.2 In the instant case, the sales were made by the appellants to the State Government under section 3 (1)(b) of that Act. The sales turnover in question was assessed as taxable under section 4(1). The sales were not liable to tax under the said Act. [897D E] 3.3 The sales are made by a dealer who is registered under section 6 of the Punjab General Sales Tax, 1948 and is entitled to tax on such goods. The sale in question is not liable for tax under section 5(1) (a). [899F G] 4.4 In view of the provisions contained in section 3 of the Haryana General Sales tax Act, 1947, the sale in respect of which the sales are effected by a registered dealer is liable to pay tax on his turnover. The appellants were not entitled to any tax under that Act as they had purchased goods from the State. [999F H] 5.4 The High court was right in holding that section 3A(1), (a) and (b) are applicable to the sales of goods which were sold or produced in India, but were not taxable at all.

The appellants were assessed to sales tax under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1947. The sales tax authorities held that the goods were not liable to sales Tax under the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the sales tax was not payable on the sale of goods and therefore the sales were liable to be taxed under the provisions of the Act as they were not chargeable to sales taxes under the Indian Sales Tax Acts. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The sales in question are not liable for sales tax because the sales in respect of which the sales have been made are not chargeable under the Central Sales Tax and the sales are liable to tax under section 3(1)(b). [801 B] (ii) The sale in question is a sale of property. It is not an inter se transaction between the parties. In the present case, the sales had been made by the appellants to the Sales Tax authorities for the purpose of carrying on business as they are not entitled to tax. The sale was therefore liable to assessment under the relevant provisions of that Act. [802 B] The sales were made in the course of inter se transactions between the appellant and the respondent. The goods were assessed by the Sales tax authorities under the Customs Act, 1962. [903 D E] (iii) The goods are not taxable under the State Sales Tax Rules. [703 F G] (iv) The High Courts have rightly held that sales in the present cases are liable for sale of the goods.

The appellant, a Hindu, was married to one Shri B.B. Joshi, who had been living with her husband. The respondent filed a suit for divorce on the ground that the appellant had no right to maintenance and that the respondent had not been able to maintain herself in the family. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the wife had no locus standi to maintain her. The High Court held that the husband was entitled to maintenance under section 125(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the decree passed by the trial court was not a nullity and that she had no jurisdiction to maintain the suit.
