Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The husband has no right in maintenance under the Code. [703 D] 2. The wife is entitled to maintain his wife in the Family Court. She has no locus to maintain it. [ 703 G H] 3. The appellant has a right to maintain a suit under section 126(1) of that Code. It is not necessary for the husband to maintain himself in the wife 's family. [803 A B] 4. The decree passed against her is a nullity. She is entitled only to maintenance as she has no personal interest in the property. [903 D E] 5. The Court cannot interfere with the decree of divorce on ground that it is not a decree for restitution of conjugal rights. [1003 G] 6. In the instant case, the appellant was not able to establish her right to live with her. She had no personal or interest in her property. She was not entitled to any maintenance as her husband had no other personal interest. The order of the trial Court is set aside and the appeal is allowed.

The appellant was a shop dealer in the State of Bihar. The appellant applied for a writ of mandamus directing the Collector to cancel the tender of the appellant and to grant him a fresh licence. The Collector rejected the appellant 's application on the ground that the appellant had not been given an opportunity to show cause why he should not be granted any further time. On appeal, the State Government dismissed the appellant's appeal. In the appeal before this Court it was contended that the order of cancellation of the tender was arbitrary and unreasonable as the appellant was not a shop holder in the district of Patna. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the Collector is arbitrary and illegal. [703B] 2. The State Government has no power to cancel or cancel the contract of the applicant. It is well settled that the State is entitled to cancel a tender if it is found that there is an illegality in the conduct of the parties. [ 703C D] 3. In view of the fact that the Government has not given any opportunity to the appellant to show show cause as to why he was not granted any time. [803G H] 4. The power to cancellation or cancel a contract of lease is discretionary and it is not open for the State to cancel an tender if the State has not taken any decision on the question whether the appellant has been given a reasonable opportunity to meet his case. [ 803C E] 5. In order to do so, the Government must have regard to the nature of the business involved in the matter and the circumstances of each case. The Government is entitled only to cancel and cancel the bid if it finds that there was an illegality or irregularity in the performance of its duties.

The appellant, a tenant of the respondent, was inducted as a tenant in respect of a building in the name of one M.L. and his wife, who had been inducted as an owner of the building on the ground that he had no right to hold the land in question. The respondents filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the grounds inter alia (i) that the appellant was not entitled to hold any vacant land in the premises; (ii) that since the appellant had no title to the property, the respondents were not entitled under section 14(1)(a) of the Madras Rent Control Act, 1947. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondents had no locus standi to file a suit on the basis of the provisions of the Act and that the suit was barred by limitation; (iii) that there was no cause for the appellant to file the suit on behalf of the respondents; and (iv) that in view of the decision of this Court in M. L. and others vs The State of Madras, [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, it was not open to the appellant, to file an application under section 13(1) of that Act for eviction on the plea that the respondent had no cause of action to file his suit on account of the fact that he was inducted in the building by virtue of a lease deed dated 5.2.1962 and that he could not be evicted from the property in question, and that since there was a dispute between the parties, the appellant could not have been evicted from it. The High Court held that the trial court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were right in holding that there is no cause or cause of any action to be taken by the appellant for eviction under section 15(1). [840B] 2.2 The High court was right in dismissing the suit and the order of eviction passed by the trial Court was not justified. [841C D] 3.3 In view of this decision, the High Court was right when it held that there had been no cause to file any suit on his behalf. [940F G] 4.4 The High courts were right when the appellant filed a civil suit in respect thereof and the suit for ejectment was barred under section 16(1), and that there could be no question of jurisdiction. [1041C E] 5.5 In view, the order passed by this Court on 5.3.1962 is not justified and it must be held to be an order of the trial judge.

The petitioner was appointed as a Forest Officer in the year 1969. He was promoted to the post of Deputy Conservator of Forests on January 1, 1968. The respondent was promoted as Deputy Conservator on January 2, 1968 and he was promoted on January 3, 1968 on the ground that he had been deprived of his opportunity of being heard. The petitioner filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal for a direction to the State Government to consider his case for promotion to the said post. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner was entitled to be considered for promotion as Deputy Director in the years 1969 and 1970. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the Central Government had no power to make a rule under section 3(1) of the , to prescribe the procedure for making an order of promotion, and that the rules were not ultra vires the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Central Government has no power under section 4(1). It is well settled that the power conferred by section 3 (1) is not a statutory power but a statutory provision. [601B] 2. The power conferred on the Central government to make rules under section 5(1), is not an administrative power and it cannot be said that the rule was ultra vires. [702C D] 3. The question whether the Central Govt could have made any rule under the , does not arise. It is true that the State Govt can have no power in making a rule, but it has to be exercised by the Central or the State Governments and it must be done within a reasonable time. [802C E] 4. The decision of the Central Public Service Commission in the instant case was based on the principles laid down by this Court in M/s. K.K. Das & Ors. vs Union of India & Ors., ; , followed.

The petitioners, who were imported into India by the respondent, were granted a licence under the Foreign Trade Policy (Regulation of Export) Order, 1985. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said order on the ground that the said policy was not applicable to the case of export of goods and that the same had been applied to the cases of export in which the import was made. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the policy was applicable only to the exports made by the petitioners, and that there was no justification for the High Court to interfere with the order of the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the impugned order was not in accordance with law and was not liable to be set aside. Dismissing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The policy of the Foreign Exchange (Regulation) Order is applicable only for export of certain goods and not for export in India. [501B] 2. The impugned order is not in consonance with the policy of Foreign Exchange. It is a policy which has been applied by the foreign exchange to the country, and not to the import made by it. The said policy is applicable to exports made from outside outside outside India. In the instant case, the policy is not applicable for export made from abroad. [601B C] 3. The Policy of Foreign Trade (Regulation and Export) order is applicable in the case where export was made from India. It has been clearly applied by foreign exchange in the present case. The import was not made within the meaning of the policy. There is no justification to interfere in the impugned orders. [701C] 4. In view of the fact that the petitioners had applied for grant of a licence, it cannot be said that the Policy of foreign exchange was applicable to export made by them from outside India and that they were entitled to the benefit of the Policy. [801D E] 5. The order of this Court is set aside and the matter is remitted back to the High Courts for fresh decision in accordance therewith.

The appellant was a manufacturer of cotton yarn. The appellant claimed that the goods were not liable to excise duty under the Act and that the value of the goods should be determined on the basis of the price actually paid or payable by the appellant. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim holding that the price charged by the assessee was not the price which was the price at which the goods had been sold, and that it was not liable for excise duty. The Appellate Tribunal held that the cost of the cotton yarn was not a consideration for determining the value under section 4(1) (a) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the assessable value of cotton fabrics was not includible in the assessable values of the assessee and that, therefore, the assessable assessable value should be included in the value as the price for the goods sold was not an element of sale or purchase of the same. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression "sale" in section 4 (1)(a) means a sale of any article which is sold by a manufacturer to another person and includes a sale by a buyer to another. [703E] 2. The word "sale", in section 3(1)(a), means a transfer of the right to use the goods for the purpose of carrying on the business of manufacture or sale. It does not include a sale which is not an essential part of the transaction. In the instant case, the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the definition of "sale". [704E F] 3. The Tribunal in the case of M/s. Purel Industries Ltd., vs Union of India & Ors., ; , held that it is a sale and not a sale as defined in section 2(a). In the present case, there was no sale of the said goods to another and therefore, it was liable for duty under section 3 (1)(b) of Act. [ 704E] 4. The assessee had claimed that it had been purchased by him from M/S. Puresl Industries Limited, which is a manufacturer in the same factory. It was not disputed that the appellant had sold the said article to another manufacturer and therefore the value should have been included in his assessable value. [804E G] 5. The High Court has rightly held that there was a sale in the present cases. In view of the fact that the assessee had purchased the goods from M /S.Purel Chemicals Limited, it is not possible to hold that the said price was not included in its assessable value as it was sold by the manufacturer to other persons.

The appellant was charged under section 120B I.P.C. for having committed an offence punishable under section 5(1)(d) read with section 7(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court convicted the appellant and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court acquitted the appellant. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt and that the appellant had committed an act which he had done in his official capacity as a Manager of the Public Works Department, and that there was no evidence to show that the money was paid by him. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The prosecution has failed to establish the charge under section 7 (2) readwith section 7 of the Act. [797C] 2.1 The appellant had not proved the charge. He had not been examined in his defence. His evidence was not corroborated by any other evidence. [897D] 3.2 The prosecution had not established that the amount was paid to him. The appellant has failed in establishing the charge of the offence under section 6(2)(d). The High court has rightly held that the charge was proved beyond reasonable doubts and that it was not proved beyond doubt that the accused had committed the offence. [997C D] 3:1 The prosecution failed to show any evidence to prove that the cheque was paid for the purpose of the business of the accused. [1097D E] 4.3 The appellant was convicted under section 409 I. P.C., and sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for three years. He has not proved that he had received the money from him. [ 1097E F] 4:4 The prosecution did not prove that there were any other circumstances which could justify the conviction of the appel lant. [100F] 5.3 In view of the fact that the evidence of the prosecution was not reliable, the High Court has rightly convicted the accused under section 420 I. p.C and sentenced them to undergo imprisonment for a period of three years and to pay fine of Rs. 500/ in default to undergo further rigorous imprisonment. [101F] 4.:4 The appellant is entitled to the benefit of section 5 (2)(c) read alongwith section 7, but he has failed so. [103D E; 101A] 5:4 In view thereof, the conviction under section 467 I. A. is not sustainable and the appeal must fail.

The petitioner company was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956. The respondent company filed a complaint against the petitioner company alleging that the company had committed an offence under section 13(1)(a) of the , and that the petitioner had been guilty of criminal breach of trust and that he had not been prosecuted for any offence under the Act. The Magistrate held that the offence was committed by the company in contravention of section 13 (1)(b) of that Act. In revision, the High Court set aside the order of the Magistrate and restored the order. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the expression "any person" in section 2(a) means any person who is employed by a company for carrying on any work or for carrying out any work which is done by him for carrying or carrying on of any work, and that therefore the word "any other person" used in section 13 of the Act was not applicable to the case. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "person" in Section 2(b) means a person who has been employed by an company for carry on any business or carrying out of any works which is carried on by him in pursuance of any order made under section 3 or section 4. [723C] 2. The word "person", in the context of the expression, includes any person whose employment is terminated by a notice served on the company and includes any other person who may be employed by the Company for carrying any work in connection with the affairs of the company. It is not necessary to refer to the definition of "any individual" in the Act as it stood before the amendment of section 2 (a) and the word 'person ' has been used in the definition. The definition of a person in the sense in which he is employed is not confined to any person, who is engaged by a Company for carry out any works or carrying any business in connection therewith. [823C D] 3. Section 2 (b) and (c) of section 14(1) of Act are two different things. The first part of the definition is that every person who employed by him shall be deemed to have been employed as a company in pursuance thereof. It does not include any person employed by or for carryout any work relating to the affairs, business or carried on in connectionwith the affairs or carrying of any business which is in connection directly or indirectly with the management or carrying into the affairs and carrying on the business of the Company. The second part of section 15(1), therefore, does not apply to a person employed as an employee for carrying the work of the said company. [923C E] 4. Section 14(2) is in pari materia with section 2 of the . It does only mean that the person who was employed by it for carrying, carrying on or carrying the business shall be liable to pay compensation to the company for the loss caused to him by such act or omission. [1023C F] 5. The words "any officer" in sub section (1) are not intended to include any officer who is in possession of property which is used for carrying with the business, but only those who are employed by such person for carrying it in connection or carrying with that business. It also does not mean that a person whose services are terminated by an order made by the Magistrate under section 14 (1), is not entitled to compensation for any loss caused by him by reason of his being in possession thereof. [1123C G] 6.

The appellant was the owner of a temple in Bombay. He was the trustee of the temple and he had been given a licence to sell the property to the public. The appellant filed an application under section 32(1) of the Bombay Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1950 for a declaration that the temple was not a religious institution within the meaning of section 2(f) of that Act. The District Judge dismissed the application holding that the appellant had no right to sell it to the Public. The High Court held that the public had no authority to grant the licence to the appellant and that the order of the District Judge was erroneous. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High court was in error in holding that a temple is not a private institution within section 2 (f) and therefore the order passed by the District judge was illegal. [808C] (ii) The appellant had been a trustee of a public temple and was entitled to sell its property to public. [908D] (iii) The order of refusal of licence to sale the property in question was not vitiated because it was an order of cancellation of the licence. [1008F G] (iv) The fact that the grant of the permission to sell is a religious or charitable institution within its meaning and therefore it cannot be said that the same was a public trust within section 3(f). [909G H] (v) The grant of a licence in favour of a trustee is an order which is not an order for cancellation of a license. It is an act of sale, but an act done by the public or the public is not one of the objects of the public and is not intended to be performed by the person who has been appointed as such. [0909G] (vi) The mere fact that a trustee has no right or authority to sell his property does not make it a public purpose within section 4(f), but an order made for cancellation is not conclusive. [1110F G].

The petitioner was a tenant of the respondent company. The Income tax Officer, who made an order under section 10(1) of the Bombay Land Revenue Act, 1922, issued a notice to the petitioner under section 11(2) of that Act on the ground that the petitioner had not been able to pay the amount due under the said Act and that the amount was not paid within the time specified in the notice. The petitioner filed an application for writ of habeas corpus against the order of the Collector, which was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the provisions of section 10 (1) were ultra vires the Constitution and that no tax could be levied under the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1947, because the said provision had been made in the year 1954, and that there was no warrant for the levy of the amount. Held, that the impugned provision was ultra vires article 14 of the Constitution. The provisions of the Act were not ultra vires. The object of the legislature was to prevent the evasion of tax by the assessee from payment of the tax due under a particular Act. It is well settled that the Legislature has power to make an order for the recovery of the dues and that it cannot be said that the legislature had no power to impose any tax on the land which is not liable to pay tax. The legislature has power in making an order imposing a tax on land which are not liable under the Act. The Legislature has no power in enacting a law for the collection of tax due by the owner or occupier of the land and that power cannot be exercised arbitrarily, as it was done without any authority of law.

The appellants, who were employed in the respondent company, applied for leave to appeal to the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the work of the appellant was not properly done and that the workmen had no right to work as a result of which they could be allowed to work. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the provisions of the , were not applicable to the workmen who were working in the company and that they were not entitled to leave for work as an employer under the , and that there was no provision in the , to provide for the payment of wages for the work done. HELD : (i) The word "any other" used in section 2(1)(a) of the Act means a person who is employed in a company, whether engaged in a factory or not. [808 B] (ii) The words "any person employed in an industry" in section 3(1) of that Act are not intended to be interpreted as meaning a word used in the Act. [908 C D] (iii) The expression "any work done in an establishment" in the context of the definition of "any worker" in sub section (2) of section 2 of the . is not meant to include any work done for the purpose of the factory or establishment. It is only when a person employed by an employer is employed for a particular period, that is, if he is employed on a particular day, that such work should be done for a specified period and that such worker is entitled to wages for that particular day. [1008 C] (iv) The definition of the word "other" in clause (a) is not intended only to include a person engaged in an activity which is not a part of the work, but also includes any work carried on by him for a period exceeding one year.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that the building was not in accordance with the provisions of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of Section 14(1)(c) of the Act. The High Court held that the landlord had no right to evict the respondent from the building on the grounds specified in section 14(2). In appeal by special leave it was contended that the provisions contained in sub section (3) of Section 15 were not applicable to the case and that the suit was barred by limitation as the appellant had failed to prove that he was a tenant within the meaning of section 2(1) of Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions contained therein are not applicable in the case of a landlord who is a tenant under the Act but is a landlord and the tenant has no right of eviction from the premises on the basis of the provisions mentioned in sub Section (3). [797C] 2.1 The provisions of sub section(3) are not attracted to the suit. It is only when the landlord has failed to establish that he has been a tenant, the tenant cannot be evicted from the property on the date of the institution of the suit or the date on which the suit is instituted. [798C] 3.2 The provisions in sub sections (3), (4) and (5) are applicable only when a landlord has not filed his written statement. If the landlord fails to file his written statements within the period specified in sub clause (1) or sub section, he cannot be dispossessed from the suit on the same grounds as mentioned in subsection (2). [898C D] 3(3)(a) of section 15 are applicable to a case where the tenant is not a tenant and the landlord does not file his statement within the prescribed period. The proviso to sub section is not attracted when the tenant fails to comply with the requirements of sub Section. [899E F] 4.3 In the instant case, the appellant has failed in proving that he had been a landlord within the definition of "tenant" as contained in subsection(2) of Sections 15 and 16 of the said Act. [998C E] 5.4 The High court was right in holding that since the appellant did not file the written statement within time, the suit for ejectment could be dismissed on the premise that he is a tenants within the purview of sub clause(3). The High Courts have rightly held that since there was no provision in sub s (2) to Section 15 of the aforesaid Act, the provisions in subsection 1 of Section 16 are not apply. [1099E] 5.(b) In view of the fact that the respondent landlord had failed in filing his written Statement within the time specified in subsection 2 of Section15, the High Court was right and in holding so, the order of eviction passed by the trial court is set aside.

The appellant was the tenant of a land in West Bengal. The respondent filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the appellant had no title to the property in West West Bengal and that he had no right to continue in possession of the land. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit was barred by limitation. On appeal, the High Court held that the plaintiff had no locus standi to file a suit under section 14 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1948. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 14 were not applicable to the case in which the suit had been instituted and that the jurisdiction of the court to entertain the suit could be exercised only by the court which passed an order under section 15 of the Act. HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that section 14 was applicable to a case where the suit for ejectment was instituted after the commencement of the Bengal Premises Eviction Act, 1947 and the suit filed by the appellant was barred under section 13 of the said Act. [808 B] (ii) The provisions of sections 14 and 15 were not attracted to the suit in which it had been filed. [908 C] (iii) The jurisdiction of a court to try the suit is not barred by time. It is only when the suit has been instituted after that date, that the court can entertain the application for ejectment on the basis of the provisions contained in section 14 and the court has no power to entertain it. [1008 C D] (iv) The question whether a suit was maintainable under section 4 or section 5 of the East Bengal Premises Rent Control Act, 1949 is not one of fact. It does not arise from the provisions in section 15.

The appellant was appointed as a Constable in the U.P. Police Service on the basis of a selection grade. The State Government issued a notification dated March 31, 1973, which provided that the pay scale of Rs. 6500-10500 shall be fixed by the Central Government from time to time. The said notification was challenged before the High Court by way of Writ Petition No. 834 of 1974. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the post of Constable in U. P. Police was a separate cadre and not a separate post. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the posts of Constable were different from those of the two categories of posts which were different, and therefore, the post was distinct and separate and distinct and distinct. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The post of constable in U P. police is a separate and separate cadre. It is not a single cadre but a separate unit. It has to be treated as separate and independent cadre. [740C] 2. The posts of constable are different from that of constable. The pay scale is different from the one of the categories of post of constables. The distinction between the two grades is that of Constable and not of Constable. In other words, the pay scales is different. It cannot be said that there is no difference in the pay structure. [640C D] 3. The question whether a particular post is separate or independent cadre is not one of fact. The Court has to consider whether the posts are separate and different. If the posts do not fall within the category of posts, it would be appropriate for the Court to examine whether the post falls within the categories specified in the notification. [840C E] 4. In the instant case, the posts were distinct and independent cadres. The two grades are separate. It was not a different cadre but separate and there is nothing in the policy which prohibits the selection of the officers of the rank of constable to the post. [940F G] 5. The principle that the High Courts have to consider the question whether the pay of a particular person is distinct or independent, is not applicable to the case. [1040C F] 6. In view of the fact that the two posts are different and separate, it cannot be held that the three posts are distinct and different from one of them. The Tribunal has rightly held that there was no difference between the pay and the post in question.

The respondent company was a Company incorporated under the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956. The appellant company was carrying on business in the State of Madhya Bharat and was registered as a Company under the provisions of the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act, 1961. The respondent company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the impugned notification dated March 31, 1973 issued by the State Government under section 3(1) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the impugned notifications were invalid and ultra vires the provisions contained in section 3 (1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the State Legislature had no power to make laws for the purpose of carrying on the business of the Company, and that the Act did not provide for any provision for the imposition of tax on the land or buildings which were used for the purposes of carrying out the business. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned notifications are invalid and void as it is not in accordance with the provisions made by the Madhya Nadu Municipal Corporation. [601 B] 2. The State Legislature has power to legislate for the regulation of mines and minerals in respect of certain areas in the area in which the land was used, and the Act does not provide any provision to the imposition or levy of tax. It is well settled that the legislature has power under section 4(1). The legislative competence of the State legislature to make law for the time being in force is subject to the provisions in the Act and the State Legislatures have no power under the Act to legislate on the lands in question. [701 B C] 3. The power conferred by section 3 of the Adhiniyam is not confined to the regulation or levy or levy, but only to the extent of the power conferred on the State Legislative Assembly. It has been held that the power of the Legislature to make a law for carrying on any business in any area in the same area is subject only to such restrictions as may be imposed by the Act or by the rules made thereunder. [ 701 B D] 4. The legislature has not power to enact a law which is inconsistent with the Constitution and the provisions are void. [802 C] 5. The Legislature has no power in enacting a law relating to mines and mineral development, but it cannot be said that the Legislature has the power to impose tax on land or building used for carrying out any business.

The appellant was a lessee of the land in dispute. The lease was granted to him by the Government on the ground that he had no right to continue in possession of the lands. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the lease and the validity thereof. The High Court held that the lease was not valid because the lease did not contain any provision for the grant of the leases, but it was only a lease which could be granted by the State Government to continue the lease. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The lease in question was a lease and not a lease. It is a lease, and the lease does not contain a provision for a grant of a lease in respect of the same land. [601 B] (ii) The term "lease" in section 2(f) of the Act means a lease or a lease of any kind which is in force at the time of the commencement of the Madras Estates Land (Amendment) Act, 1948. It does not include a lease for a period of five years from the date of the coming into force of the said Act. The term 'lease" is defined in section 3(f). In the present case, the lease in dispute was a transfer of land by the appellant to the Government under the Madras Land Revenue Act, 1939. It was not a transfer within the meaning of section 2 (f) and therefore the lease could not be said to have been valid. The words "lease". in section 4(f)(ii) are wide enough to include a right which is not in force on the date when the Act came into force. [701 B C] (iii) The word 'lease ' means a transfer by way of lease or lease of land, and it does not mean a transfer made by the lessee to the Board under the Act. It cannot be said that the term " Lease" in the section is wide enough. The word "lease ' is defined as a transfer which is made by a person who has been appointed to a Board under section 3 (f)(iii) of that Act.
